It has two chapters:

The Metrics Cookbook defines commonly used metrics, including their calculation logic and example SQL queries.

title: Site Uptime
text:
The rolling-window uptime percentage for each monitored CanadaLogin site, showing what proportion of five-minute pings succeeded over each time horizon.
Six sites are monitored: the two public-facing login pages (EN/FR), the Manage Profile app (staging and production), and the IdP (staging and production).

title: Site Uptime
text:
Calculation
Filter to the most recent date partition and read the precomputed rolling-window uptime columns from sre.uptime_summary. Each uptime_* column is already a percentage (0-100), calculated from all five-minute pings over the named window.
To track uptime over time for a specific site, remove the MAX(date) filter and group by date.






Warning



Upstream monitoring gap (July 28 – September 23, 2026): External synthetic health checks in cds-snc/status-statut halted during this ~8-week window. Because zero down minutes were recorded across zero executed pings, sre.uptime_summary defaulted to reporting uptime_day = 100.0% with response_day_ms = 0.

When aggregating daily uptime or querying historical trends, filter out unmonitored days using WHERE response_day_ms > 0.
In snapshot queries, treat response_day_ms = 0 (or NULL) as unmonitored rather than confirmed 100% availability.









NoteExample queries






SQLR


Latest snapshot, all sites, all rolling windows:
SELECT
    slug,
    lang,
    status,
    uptime_day,
    uptime_week,
    uptime_month,
    uptime_year,
    uptime_alltime
FROM sre.uptime_summary
WHERE date = (SELECT MAX(date) FROM sre.uptime_summary)
ORDER BY slug;
Trend over time, year uptime for a specific site:
SELECT
    date,
    uptime_year,
    uptime_alltime
FROM sre.uptime_summary
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE slug = 'canada-login-website-en'
  AND CAST(date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-06-30'
  -- exclude dates where upstream monitoring was inactive
  AND response_day_ms > 0
ORDER BY date;


Latest snapshot, all sites, all rolling windows:
uptime_s <- tbl(con, in_schema("sre", "uptime_summary"))
latest_date <- uptime_s |> summarise(d = max(date, na.rm = TRUE)) |> pull(d)

uptime_s |>
  filter(as.Date(date) == as.Date(latest_date)) |>
  select(slug, lang, status, uptime_day, uptime_week, uptime_month,
         uptime_year, uptime_alltime) |>
  arrange(slug)
Trend over time, year uptime for a specific site:
tbl(con, in_schema("sre", "uptime_summary")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    slug == "canada-login-website-en",
    as.Date(date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date) <= as.Date("2026-06-30"),
    # exclude dates where upstream monitoring was inactive
    response_day_ms > 0
  ) |>
  select(date, uptime_year, uptime_alltime) |>
  arrange(date)

title: Site Uptime
text:
Interpretation notes
The uptime windows are rolling, not calendar-aligned. uptime_month on a given date covers the 30 days trailing that date’s stats update (~23:2x UTC), not a fixed calendar month. To aggregate by calendar month, group by substr(date, 1, 7).
Rolling windows (uptime_week, uptime_month, uptime_year, uptime_alltime) spanning the July 28 – September 23, 2026 gap incorporate unmonitored days recorded as 100% uptime, which may slightly elevate rolling availability figures.

title: Outage Events
text: Individual site outage events detected by the uptime monitor: when a site went down, when it recovered, and the HTTP status code at time of detection.

title: Outage Events
text:
Calculation
Filter sre.uptime_timeseries to rows where status = 'down'. Each such row represents a moment when the upptime bot detected the site was unreachable and committed that state to the history file.
To count outage events per site over a reporting period, group the filtered rows by slug and count.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


All outage events in a reporting period:
SELECT
    date,
    ping_timestamp,
    slug,
    lang,
    http_code,
    response_ms
FROM sre.uptime_timeseries
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE status = 'down'
  AND CAST(date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-06-30'
ORDER BY date DESC, slug;
Outage event count per site in a reporting period:
SELECT
    slug,
    lang,
    COUNT(*) AS outage_event_count
FROM sre.uptime_timeseries
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE status = 'down'
  AND CAST(date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-06-30'
GROUP BY slug, lang
ORDER BY outage_event_count DESC;


All outage events in a reporting period:
tbl(con, in_schema("sre", "uptime_timeseries")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    status == "down",
    as.Date(date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date) <= as.Date("2026-06-30")
  ) |>
  select(date, ping_timestamp, slug, lang, http_code, response_ms) |>
  arrange(desc(date), slug)
Outage event count per site in a reporting period:
tbl(con, in_schema("sre", "uptime_timeseries")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    status == "down",
    as.Date(date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date) <= as.Date("2026-06-30")
  ) |>
  count(slug, lang, name = "outage_event_count") |>
  arrange(desc(outage_event_count))

title: Outage Events
text:
Interpretation notes
Each row in sre.uptime_timeseries is a single commit by the upptime bot. On a normal all-up day there is one row per site (the daily ~23:2x UTC snapshot). On an outage day there are additional rows (one when the site went down and one when it recovered), so status = 'down' rows count detection events, not total minutes of downtime. For total outage duration, use the daily_minutes_down JSON field in sre.uptime_summary.
During the July 28 – September 23, 2026 upstream monitoring outage, zero ping commits were executed. The absence of status = 'down' rows during that window reflects inactive synthetic monitoring rather than confirmed 100% uptime.

title: Weekly Ticket Volume
text: The total number of PSOM tickets captured in each Monday snapshot, showing how the number of tickets in the project changes over time.

title: Weekly Ticket Volume
text:
Calculation
Keep only the Monday date partitions and count the rows in each. The snapshot ran weekly on Mondays until 2026-09-28 and nightly from 2026-09-29, so filtering to Mondays gives one comparable total per week across the whole history.
For a finer view from 2026-09-29 on, count every partition: there is one per night.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


By week:
SELECT
    date,
    COUNT(*) AS ticket_count
FROM jira.psom
WHERE day_of_week(CAST(date AS DATE)) = 1
GROUP BY date
ORDER BY date DESC;
By day, from the first nightly snapshot:
SELECT
    date,
    COUNT(*) AS ticket_count
FROM jira.psom
WHERE CAST(date AS DATE) >= DATE '2026-09-29'
GROUP BY date
ORDER BY date DESC;


By week:
tbl(con, in_schema("jira", "psom")) |>
  filter(wday(as.Date(date), week_start = 1) == 1) |>
  count(date, name = "ticket_count") |>
  arrange(desc(date))
By day, from the first nightly snapshot:
tbl(con, in_schema("jira", "psom")) |>
  filter(as.Date(date) >= as.Date("2026-09-29")) |>
  count(date, name = "ticket_count") |>
  arrange(desc(date))

title: Weekly Ticket Volume
text:
Interpretation notes
This counts the tickets still in the project on each Monday, not the tickets opened that week or the open backlog; for those, see Tickets Opened, Closed, and Open. It includes Done and Canceled tickets until they are archived, and it drops when a batch of tickets is archived (from 52 to 25 between 2026-09-14 and 2026-09-21). The first snapshot, 2026-06-30, was a Tuesday, so the filter leaves it out.

title: SLA PSO Time-to-Done Breach Rate
text:
The proportion of PSOM tickets that missed the “Time to Done - PSO” SLA, based on the latest snapshot.
This metric reflects how well the PSO team is resolving tickets within the agreed timeframe, counting only the time the ticket is with that team. Unlike the whole-ticket SLA Time-to-Done Breach Rate, its clock pauses while the ticket is escalated. Like that SLA, it also pauses while waiting for the customer. Only tickets where the SLA clock started are included; tickets with no clock are excluded.

title: SLA PSO Time-to-Done Breach Rate
text:
Calculation
From jira.psom_sla, filter to the most recent date partition, to sla = 'pso_time_to_done', and to rows where breached is not null (i.e., the clock started). Divide the count of rows where breached is true by the total count of those rows.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS total_sla_tickets,
    SUM(CASE WHEN breached THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS breached_count,
    CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN breached THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0) AS breach_rate
FROM jira.psom_sla
WHERE date = (SELECT MAX(date) FROM jira.psom_sla)
  AND sla = 'pso_time_to_done'
  AND breached IS NOT NULL;


psom_sla <- tbl(con, in_schema("jira", "psom_sla"))
latest_date <- psom_sla |> summarise(d = max(date, na.rm = TRUE)) |> pull(d)

psom_sla |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date) == as.Date(latest_date),
    sla == "pso_time_to_done",
    !is.na(breached)
  ) |>
  summarise(
    total_sla_tickets = n(),
    breached_count    = sum(as.integer(breached), na.rm = TRUE),
    breach_rate       = sum(as.integer(breached), na.rm = TRUE) / as.double(n())
  )

title: SLA PSO Time-to-Done Breach Rate
text:
Interpretation notes
The rate is a proportion between 0 and 1. Tickets whose clock never started (null breached) are excluded from both numerator and denominator. Check total_sla_tickets to understand the sample size underlying the rate.
This clock only started on tickets created from about 2026-08-06, and the older snapshots have no pso_time_to_done rows, so the sample is smaller than for the other SLAs. The goal is set per ticket and counted in working hours (09:00 to 17:00), so a breach means the ticket missed its own target.
A ticket that is still open and inside its goal is recorded as not breached (false), the same as a ticket that met the SLA. The rate on a live snapshot is therefore a lower bound: some of those open tickets may still breach before they are resolved. It is most meaningful once the snapshot’s tickets are largely resolved.

title: SMS Code Entry Rate
text:
The proportion of SMS one-time codes sent over a selected reporting period that someone went on to enter correctly.
This is the clearest signal of automated traffic in the MFA data. Bots that request codes they cannot read drive codes sent up without codes entered, so the entry rate falls on those days while the MFA Success Rate barely moves.
The two rates have different denominators. The success rate divides successes by attempts (success plus failure), so a code that is never entered does not appear in it at all. The entry rate divides successes by codes sent, so every unentered code counts against it. Do not quote one as the other: on a typical day the entry rate sits far below the success rate.

title: SMS Code Entry Rate
text:
Calculation
Restrict to mfa_type = 'sms_otp'. Divide the sum of count where result = 'success' by the sum of count where result = 'sent'. To see a bot day, compute it per day rather than over the whole window.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


Overall:
SELECT
    CAST(SUM(count) FILTER (WHERE result = 'success') AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(count) FILTER (WHERE result = 'sent'), 0)
        AS sms_code_entry_rate
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_mfa_activity
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
  AND mfa_type = 'sms_otp';
By day:
SELECT
    CAST(from_date AS DATE) AS day,
    SUM(count) FILTER (WHERE result = 'sent') AS sms_codes_sent,
    SUM(count) FILTER (WHERE result = 'success') AS sms_codes_entered,
    CAST(SUM(count) FILTER (WHERE result = 'success') AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(count) FILTER (WHERE result = 'sent'), 0)
        AS sms_code_entry_rate
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_mfa_activity
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
  AND mfa_type = 'sms_otp'
GROUP BY CAST(from_date AS DATE)
ORDER BY day;


Overall:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_mfa_activity")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-05-28"),
    mfa_type == "sms_otp"
  ) |>
  summarise(
    sms_code_entry_rate =
      sum(if_else(result == "success", as.double(count), 0), na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(if_else(result == "sent", as.double(count), 0), na.rm = TRUE)
  )
By day:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_mfa_activity")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-05-28"),
    mfa_type == "sms_otp"
  ) |>
  mutate(day = as.Date(from_date)) |>
  group_by(day) |>
  summarise(
    sms_codes_sent = sum(if_else(result == "sent", count, 0L), na.rm = TRUE),
    sms_codes_entered =
      sum(if_else(result == "success", count, 0L), na.rm = TRUE),
    sms_code_entry_rate =
      sum(if_else(result == "success", as.double(count), 0), na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(if_else(result == "sent", as.double(count), 0), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(day)

title: Sign-up Email Code Speed
text:
How quickly people enter the code CanadaLogin emails them during sign-up, as the median seconds from the code being sent to it being entered, per day.
A person has to open their inbox, find the message, and type the code, which takes a while. A bot reading the mailbox programmatically does it in a few seconds, so a day whose median drops sharply is a sign of automated sign-ups. This is a detection signal: the Automated Traffic dashboard holds the thresholds that turn it into a flag.
It reads the raw event stream, because the summary table has no timestamps.

title: Sign-up Email Code Speed
text:
Calculation
Take Email OTP events from the sign-up client (performedby_type = 'api'). Link each code to its entry through the hashed email address, mfadevice, leaving out a blank or UNKNOWN one: order each address’s events by time, and keep a success whose previous event was a sent. That pairs an entry with the code sent just before it, and drops a success after a failure, which would otherwise time the retry rather than the code.
The time to enter is the seconds between the two, rounded down and capped at 600, so one code left overnight cannot drag a day’s figures. Report each ET day’s codes entered and the median of their times. The median is the lower median: the smallest time with at least half the day’s codes at or below it.
Filter on the UTC year, month, and day partitions, and read one UTC day either side of the window: an ET day ends at 04:00 or 05:00 UTC the next day, and a code entered early in the window may have been sent the day before. Times are whole seconds, so a code sent and entered in the same second tie; order by result as well, which puts sent first.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


WITH events AS (
    SELECT
        mfadevice,
        result,
        from_iso8601_timestamp(replace(substr(time, 1, 19), ' ', 'T') || 'Z') AS at
    FROM ibm_verify_events_raw.mfa_activity
    -- UTC partitions: the window, plus one day either side
    WHERE year = '2026'
      AND (month = '09' OR (month = '08' AND day = '31') OR (month = '10' AND day = '01'))
      AND mfamethod = 'Email OTP'
      -- the sign-up client
      AND performedby_type = 'api'
      AND mfadevice NOT IN ('', 'UNKNOWN', 'Unknown')
),
paired AS (
    SELECT
        result,
        at,
        -- result breaks a tie within one second: "sent" sorts before "success"
        lag(result) OVER (PARTITION BY mfadevice ORDER BY at, result) AS prev_result,
        lag(at) OVER (PARTITION BY mfadevice ORDER BY at, result) AS prev_at
    FROM events
),
entries AS (
    SELECT
        date(at_timezone(at, 'America/Toronto')) AS day,
        -- whole seconds, capped so one late entry cannot skew the day
        least(floor(to_unixtime(at) - to_unixtime(prev_at)), 600) AS seconds
    FROM paired
    WHERE result = 'success' AND prev_result = 'sent'
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT
        day,
        seconds,
        count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY day) AS codes_entered,
        row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY day ORDER BY seconds) AS position
    FROM entries
)

SELECT
    day,
    max(codes_entered) AS codes_entered,
    -- the lower median: the first time at or past half the day's codes
    min(seconds) FILTER (WHERE position >= codes_entered / 2.0) AS median_seconds
FROM ranked
-- set the reporting window in ET days; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE day BETWEEN DATE '2026-09-01' AND DATE '2026-09-30'
GROUP BY day
ORDER BY day;


tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_raw", "mfa_activity")) |>
  # UTC partitions: the window, plus one day either side
  filter(
    year == "2026",
    month == "09" | (month == "08" & day == "31") | (month == "10" & day == "01"),
    mfamethod == "Email OTP",
    # the sign-up client
    performedby_type == "api",
    !mfadevice %in% c("", "UNKNOWN", "Unknown")
  ) |>
  mutate(at = sql("from_iso8601_timestamp(replace(substr(time, 1, 19), ' ', 'T') || 'Z')")) |>
  group_by(mfadevice) |>
  # result breaks a tie within one second: "sent" sorts before "success"
  window_order(at, result) |>
  mutate(prev_result = lag(result), prev_at = lag(at)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(result == "success", prev_result == "sent") |>
  mutate(
    day = sql("date(at_timezone(at, 'America/Toronto'))"),
    # whole seconds, capped so one late entry cannot skew the day
    seconds = sql("least(floor(to_unixtime(at) - to_unixtime(prev_at)), 600)")
  ) |>
  group_by(day) |>
  # counted before ordering, so it is the day's total, not a running count
  mutate(codes_entered = n()) |>
  window_order(seconds) |>
  mutate(position = row_number()) |>
  # set the reporting window in ET days; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(day >= as.Date("2026-09-01"), day <= as.Date("2026-09-30")) |>
  summarise(
    codes_entered = max(codes_entered, na.rm = TRUE),
    # the lower median: the first time at or past half the day's codes
    median_seconds = min(if_else(position >= codes_entered / 2, seconds, NA), na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(day)

title: Sign-up Email Code Speed
text:
Interpretation notes
Read the median next to the count. A fast median on a day with few codes is noise; a fast median on a day with many more codes than usual is the pattern bot sign-ups leave. The cap means a median of 600 seconds says “10 minutes or more”, not exactly 10 minutes.
Only first-try entries are timed. A success after a failure is left out, so someone who mistyped the code once does not count. That keeps the figure about reading the email, not about typing.
It is expensive for long windows. The query reads the raw table. Keep the partition filter to the months you need.

title: Sign-Ins per Active User (Estimated)
text:
How often a typical user signs in to CanadaLogin over a calendar month, counting only the users who signed in at all that month.
This builds on Completed Sign-In Sessions and inherits its estimate and its assumptions. The denominator is mtd_unique_users read on the month’s last day, so the reporting window has to be whole calendar months.

title: Sign-Ins per Active User (Estimated)
text:
Calculation
Per calendar month, estimate sessions as in Completed Sign-In Sessions: sum successful_logins and subtract the successes of the factors that can complete a sign-in (sms_otp, voice_otp, fido2). Divide by mtd_unique_users on the month’s last day, which is that month’s distinct signed-in users.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


WITH first_factor AS (
    SELECT
        date_trunc('month', CAST(from_date AS DATE)) AS month,
        SUM(successful_logins) AS successful_events
    FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_auth_total_logins
    -- set the reporting window; whole calendar months only
    WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-05-01' AND DATE '2026-08-31'
    GROUP BY 1
),

second_factor AS (
    SELECT
        date_trunc('month', CAST(from_date AS DATE)) AS month,
        SUM(count) AS mfa_successes
    FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_mfa_activity
    -- set the reporting window; whole calendar months only
    WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-05-01' AND DATE '2026-08-31'
      -- outcome events only; a "sent" OTP is an issuance, not a success
      AND result = 'success'
      -- email_otp validates an email address at sign-up and never enters
      -- successful_logins, so subtracting it would over-correct
      AND mfa_type IN ('sms_otp', 'voice_otp', 'fido2')
    GROUP BY 1
),

active_users AS (
    SELECT month, mtd_unique_users AS monthly_active_users
    FROM (
        SELECT
            date_trunc('month', CAST(from_date AS DATE)) AS month,
            mtd_unique_users,
            ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
                PARTITION BY date_trunc('month', CAST(from_date AS DATE))
                ORDER BY from_date DESC
            ) AS day_rank
        FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_auth_total_logins
        -- set the reporting window; whole calendar months only
        WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-05-01' AND DATE '2026-08-31'
    )
    -- mtd_unique_users accumulates through the month, so the last day holds
    -- the month's distinct signed-in users
    WHERE day_rank = 1
)

SELECT
    first_factor.month,
    first_factor.successful_events - second_factor.mfa_successes
        AS estimated_sessions,
    active_users.monthly_active_users,
    CAST(
        first_factor.successful_events - second_factor.mfa_successes AS DOUBLE
    ) / NULLIF(active_users.monthly_active_users, 0)
        AS sign_ins_per_active_user
FROM first_factor
JOIN second_factor ON first_factor.month = second_factor.month
JOIN active_users ON first_factor.month = active_users.month
ORDER BY first_factor.month;


sign_in_types <- c("sms_otp", "voice_otp", "fido2")

first_factor <- tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_auth_total_logins")) |>
  # set the reporting window; whole calendar months only
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-05-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-08-31")
  ) |>
  group_by(month = floor_date(as.Date(from_date), "month")) |>
  summarise(successful_events = sum(as.double(successful_logins), na.rm = TRUE))

second_factor <- tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_mfa_activity")) |>
  # set the reporting window; whole calendar months only
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-05-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-08-31"),
    # outcome events only; a "sent" OTP is an issuance, not a success
    result == "success",
    # email_otp validates an email address at sign-up and never enters
    # successful_logins, so subtracting it would over-correct
    mfa_type %in% sign_in_types
  ) |>
  group_by(month = floor_date(as.Date(from_date), "month")) |>
  summarise(mfa_successes = sum(as.double(count), na.rm = TRUE))

active_users <- tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_auth_total_logins")) |>
  # set the reporting window; whole calendar months only
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-05-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-08-31")
  ) |>
  group_by(month = floor_date(as.Date(from_date), "month")) |>
  # mtd_unique_users accumulates through the month, so the last day holds
  # the month's distinct signed-in users
  filter(from_date == max(from_date, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(month, monthly_active_users = mtd_unique_users)

first_factor |>
  inner_join(second_factor, by = "month") |>
  inner_join(active_users, by = "month") |>
  mutate(
    estimated_sessions = successful_events - mfa_successes,
    sign_ins_per_active_user =
      as.double(estimated_sessions) / as.double(monthly_active_users)
  ) |>
  select(month, estimated_sessions, monthly_active_users, sign_ins_per_active_user) |>
  arrange(month)

title: Authentication Success Rate
text:
The proportion of authentication attempts that succeeded, across all of CanadaLogin. A failed attempt can be a wrong password or a failed second factor.
This metric is useful for monitoring overall authentication health. A sustained drop can indicate a service problem, a misconfigured application, or elevated attack traffic inflating the failure count.

title: Authentication Success Rate
text:
Calculation
Divide the sum of successful_logins by the sum of all attempts (successful_logins + failed_logins) over the selected reporting period.
To track the metric over time, bin the same calculation by week. Truncating from_date to the week groups each day into its Monday-anchored bin, so the result is one success rate per Monday-to-Sunday week.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


Overall:
SELECT
    CAST(SUM(successful_logins) AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(successful_logins + failed_logins), 0) AS authentication_success_rate
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_auth_total_logins
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28';
By week:
SELECT
    date_trunc('week', CAST(from_date AS DATE)) AS week_start,
    CAST(SUM(successful_logins) AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(successful_logins + failed_logins), 0) AS authentication_success_rate
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_auth_total_logins
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
-- date_trunc('week', ...) anchors each bin to its Monday
GROUP BY date_trunc('week', CAST(from_date AS DATE))
ORDER BY week_start;

  ) |>

      sum(as.double(successful_logins), na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(successful_logins + failed_logins, na.rm = TRUE)

By week:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_auth_total_logins")) |>

  filter(

title: Authentication Success Rate
text:
Interpretation notes
The rate is a proportion between 0 and 1. Read it alongside authentication event volume: a low success rate on very low volume may just be noise, while the same rate on high volume is a real signal. In the weekly view, the first and last weeks of the reporting window are usually partial (the window rarely starts or ends on a Monday), so treat boundary weeks with caution when comparing trends.
This rate is computed over authentication methods, not sessions. When signing in to CanadaLogin, IBM Verify records each method as its own event, so a mistyped password is a failed event even when the user then succeeds and completes the sign-in (see the events_auth_total_logins caveat). The figure measures how often individual authentication steps succeed, not how often a sign-in ultimately completes. The per-application rate counts a different IBM Verify event type, the handoff to a relying party with no factors entered, so the two rates are not comparable.

title: Sign-in MFA Activity by Factor
text:
The volume of MFA challenges across the factors the public can use to sign in, with each factor’s share of the total.
Where All MFA Activity by Factor covers every factor type the platform records, this metric keeps only the ones a member of the public can present as a second factor when signing in: sms_otp, voice_otp, and, since passkeys became generally available on 2026-07-06, fido2. The internal and administrative factors that dominate the platform-wide view are left out.
IBM Verify files MFA as a subtype of the authentication event rather than as an event type of its own, so these counts are a slice of the CanadaLogin-wide authentication events, not an independent stream.
Two factors that reach the public are deliberately excluded:

title: Sign-in MFA Activity by Factor
text:
Calculation
Restrict to the sign-in factors (sms_otp, voice_otp, fido2), then, as in All MFA Activity by Factor, de-duplicate before counting: the OTP factors (sms_otp, voice_otp) record both a sent event and a subsequent success/failure event for the same challenge, so only the sent row is counted for these; fido2 (passkeys) has no sent event and is counted through its success/failure rows. Sum count grouped by mfa_type, then divide each factor’s total by the combined total to get its share.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    mfa_type,
    SUM(count) AS mfa_challenges,
    CAST(SUM(count) AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(SUM(count)) OVER (), 0) AS factor_share
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_mfa_activity
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
  -- restrict to the factors the public can use to sign in. email_otp is
  -- excluded because it only validates emails at sign-up, and kq, totp, qr,
  -- and ibm_verify_push are internal factors, not public sign-in options.
  AND mfa_type IN ('sms_otp', 'voice_otp', 'fido2')
  -- de-duplicate OTP challenges: count only "sent" for the OTP factors
  -- (sms_otp, voice_otp), and "success"/"failure" for fido2 (passkeys),
  -- which has no "sent" event.
  AND (
    result = 'sent'
    OR (
      result IN ('success', 'failure')
      AND mfa_type NOT IN ('sms_otp', 'email_otp', 'voice_otp')
    )
  )
GROUP BY mfa_type
ORDER BY mfa_challenges DESC;


otp_types <- c("sms_otp", "email_otp", "voice_otp")
sign_in_types <- c("sms_otp", "voice_otp", "fido2")

tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_mfa_activity")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-05-28"),
    # restrict to the factors the public can use to sign in. email_otp is
    # excluded because it only validates emails at sign-up, and kq, totp, qr,
    # and ibm_verify_push are internal factors, not public sign-in options.
    mfa_type %in% sign_in_types,
    # de-duplicate OTP challenges: count only "sent" for the OTP factors
    # (sms_otp, voice_otp), and "success"/"failure" for fido2 (passkeys),
    # which has no "sent" event.
    result == "sent" |
      (result %in% c("success", "failure") & !mfa_type %in% otp_types)
  ) |>
  group_by(mfa_type) |>
  summarise(
    mfa_challenges = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    factor_share =
      as.double(mfa_challenges) / sum(mfa_challenges, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mfa_challenges))

title: Sign-in MFA Activity by Factor
text:
Interpretation notes
factor_share is a proportion between 0 and 1 and sums to 1 across these factors only, so it is not comparable to the shares in All MFA Activity by Factor, which are taken over every factor.
Do not quote factor_share as passkey uptake. It is not like for like across factors: an SMS code counts once it is sent, entered or not, while a passkey prompt counts only once it reaches an outcome, so passkeys read low. For uptake, use Sign-in Factor Share of Successes.
Passkey (fido2) activity appears only from the 2026-07-06 rollout onward, so a reporting window that predates that date will show little or none.

title: Second-factor Attempts
text:
The number of times someone presented a second factor at sign-in over a selected reporting period, whether it succeeded or failed.
An attempt is an outcome: a code entered, right or wrong, or a passkey prompt that succeeded or failed. A code that was sent and never entered is not an attempt; it is still a challenge. This is the denominator of MFA Success Rate, so the two always agree.
It covers the factors the public can sign in with: sms_otp, voice_otp, and fido2 (passkeys). email_otp checks an email address at sign-up and is not a second factor, and kq, totp, qr, and ibm_verify_push are internal.

title: Second-factor Attempts
text:
Calculation
Restrict to the sign-in factors and to the success and failure rows, then sum count. Leave out sent rows: they are issued codes, not outcomes.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    SUM(count) AS second_factor_attempts
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_mfa_activity
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
  -- the factors the public can sign in with; email_otp is a sign-up check
  AND mfa_type IN ('sms_otp', 'voice_otp', 'fido2')
  -- outcomes only; a "sent" row is a code issued, not an attempt
  AND result IN ('success', 'failure');


tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_mfa_activity")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-05-28"),
    # the factors the public can sign in with; email_otp is a sign-up check
    mfa_type %in% c("sms_otp", "voice_otp", "fido2"),
    # outcomes only; a "sent" row is a code issued, not an attempt
    result %in% c("success", "failure")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    second_factor_attempts = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

title: Second-factor Attempts
text:
Interpretation notes
Attempts count tries, not people: someone who mistypes a code twice and then gets it right makes three attempts. Failed attempts are attempts less successes. For the codes issued, whether or not anyone entered them, use MFA Challenges.

title: New Accounts and Idle Account Rate
text:
New CanadaLogin accounts per day, and how many of them never used a partner service. A jump in the idle rate is a sign of bot sign-ups.
This is the one IBM Verify metric that reads the raw event stream, because no summary table records when an account first appears.

title: New Accounts and Idle Account Rate
text:
Interpretation notes
Idle accounts are a signal, not a bot count. Some real people sign up and never use a service. Normal days run about 10% to 15% idle. On bot-wave days, nearly all new accounts are idle.
Pick the window for the question. To spot a bot day, use the same-day rate: it is final the next morning. To compare months, use the 14-day rate: the “ever” rate keeps falling as accounts have more time to reach a service, so recent days look worse than old ones, and the last 14 days of any window are still provisional on the 14-day rate.
New accounts add up across days, rates do not. Each account has one creation day, so summing new_accounts or idle_accounts over days is correct. Recompute a rate over a longer window from the summed counts.
Since launch is point in time. An account leaves the idle count on the day it first uses a public service, and earlier days are never restated. So the idle count on a past day is what it was on that day, not how many of those accounts are still idle now. The other choice, restating history, would shrink every past day’s idle count as accounts later reach a service.
When an account appears. Most new accounts first appear with a successful password, which suggests the sign-up flow signs an account in once the password is set, before any MFA. A few first appear through a token exchange instead, possibly migrated accounts. Both readings are observed, not confirmed with the sign-up flow’s owners.
It is expensive. The query reads both raw tables from launch, and the cost grows every month. Run it for a reporting window, not on a schedule.

title: MFA Success Rate by Factor
text:
The MFA success rate broken down by factor type, so that factors can be compared against one another.
This metric is useful for spotting whether one second factor is notably easier to clear than another. Because the rate is calculated per attempt, a factor that users frequently mistype before getting right (common with OTP factors) shows a lower rate, which is the friction signal you want when comparing ease of use.

title: MFA Success Rate by Factor
text:
Calculation
Within each mfa_type, divide the sum of count where result = 'success' by the sum of count where result is 'success' or 'failure'. As with the overall MFA Success Rate, sent rows are excluded from both the numerator and the denominator because they are not outcomes. mfa_attempts is the denominator (successes plus failures) and is reported alongside the rate so that low-volume factors, whose rates are noisy, can be discounted.
Note that mfa_attempts here counts success and failure events only. It is not the de-duplicated usage volume reported by All MFA Activity by Factor, which counts sent events for OTP factors instead.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


By factor:
SELECT
    mfa_type,
    SUM(count) AS mfa_attempts,
    CAST(SUM(count) FILTER (WHERE result = 'success') AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(count), 0) AS mfa_success_rate
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_mfa_activity
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
  -- exclude "sent" rows; success rate is calculated from outcome events only.
  -- including "sent" would inflate the denominator and deflate the rate.
  AND result IN ('success', 'failure')
GROUP BY mfa_type
ORDER BY mfa_attempts DESC;
By factor and week:
SELECT
    date_trunc('week', CAST(from_date AS DATE)) AS week_start,
    mfa_type,
    SUM(count) AS mfa_attempts,
    CAST(SUM(count) FILTER (WHERE result = 'success') AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(count), 0) AS mfa_success_rate
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_mfa_activity
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
  AND result IN ('success', 'failure')
-- date_trunc('week', ...) anchors each bin to its Monday
GROUP BY date_trunc('week', CAST(from_date AS DATE)), mfa_type
ORDER BY week_start, mfa_type;


By factor:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_mfa_activity")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-05-28"),
    # exclude "sent" rows; success rate is calculated from outcome events only.
    # including "sent" would inflate the denominator and deflate the rate.
    result %in% c("success", "failure")
  ) |>
  group_by(mfa_type) |>
  summarise(
    mfa_attempts = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE),
    mfa_success_rate =
      sum(if_else(result == "success", as.double(count), 0), na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(count, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mfa_attempts))
By factor and week:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_mfa_activity")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-05-28"),
    result %in% c("success", "failure")
  ) |>
  # floor_date(..., "week") translates to Athena's date_trunc('week', ...),
  # which anchors each bin to its Monday
  mutate(week_start = floor_date(as.Date(from_date), "week")) |>
  group_by(week_start, mfa_type) |>
  summarise(
    mfa_attempts = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE),
    mfa_success_rate =
      sum(if_else(result == "success", as.double(count), 0), na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(count, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(week_start, mfa_type)

In the weekly view, the first and last weeks of the reporting window are usually partial (the window rarely starts or ends on a Monday), so treat boundary weeks with caution when comparing trends.

title: All MFA Activity by Factor
text:
The volume of MFA challenges broken down by factor type, with each factor’s share of total activity. This is the platform-wide view: it covers every factor type the system records, including the internal and administrative factors (kq, totp, qr, ibm_verify_push) and the email_otp factor used only to validate emails at sign-up. For usage restricted to the factors the public can sign in with, see Sign-in MFA Activity by Factor.
This metric shows which second factors are exercised across the whole platform. Historically the mix has been dominated by sms_otp and email_otp.   -- "success"/"failure" for non-OTP types (which have no "sent" event).
  AND (
    result = 'sent'
    OR (
      result IN ('success', 'failure')
      AND mfa_type NOT IN ('sms_otp', 'email_otp', 'voice_otp')

title: Cumulative Unique Users by Application
text:
The number of distinct users observed for each application over a chosen reporting window: this month or this calendar year.
The cumulative unique-user columns increase or remain stable over time. This metric is closer to “how many distinct people have used the application in this window” than the daily unique user metrics.

title: Cumulative Unique Users by Application
text:
Calculation
Take the latest value of the cumulative unique-user column over the selected window, grouped by application. The window is chosen by which column you read (see the note on reporting timespans):

mtd_unique_users for month-to-date
ytd_unique_users for year-to-date

The WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN ... bounds set the “as of” reporting date; the most recent row in the window holds the current cumulative total.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


Month-to-date:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT
        application_name,
        from_date,
        mtd_unique_users,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY application_name
            ORDER BY from_date DESC
        ) AS rn
    FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_app_login_counts
    WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-06-01' AND DATE '2026-06-08'
    -- to exclude internal applications from adoption reporting, uncomment:
    -- AND application_name NOT IN (
    --     SELECT al.alias
    --     FROM   rp.alias al
    --     JOIN   rp.service s ON al.rp_id = s.rp_id
    --     WHERE  s.is_internal
    -- )
)

SELECT
    application_name,
    mtd_unique_users
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY mtd_unique_users DESC;
Year-to-date:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT
        application_name,
        from_date,
        ytd_unique_users,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY application_name
            ORDER BY from_date DESC
        ) AS rn
    FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_app_login_counts
    WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-06-08'
    -- to exclude internal applications from adoption reporting, uncomment:
    -- AND application_name NOT IN (
    --     SELECT al.alias
    --     FROM   rp.alias al
    --     JOIN   rp.service s ON al.rp_id = s.rp_id
    --     WHERE  s.is_internal
    -- )
)

SELECT
    application_name,
    ytd_unique_users
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY ytd_unique_users DESC;


Month-to-date:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_app_login_counts")) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-06-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-06-08")

  # to exclude internal applications from adoption reporting, uncomment:
  # anti_join(
  #   tbl(con, in_schema("rp", "alias")) |>

    from_date,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE

    application_name,
    mtd_unique_users

tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_app_login_counts")) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-06-08")
  ) |>
  # to exclude internal applications from adoption reporting, uncomment:
  # anti_join(
  #   tbl(con, in_schema("rp", "alias")) |>

title: Average Daily Users
text:
How many distinct users signed in to CanadaLogin on a typical day over a selected reporting window: the mean of the daily unique-user counts.
It is a typical day, not reach. An average of 2,000 daily users over four weeks does not mean 2,000 people used CanadaLogin in those four weeks; the same person on ten different days counts on all ten. For how many different people used it, read a cumulative column (see Cumulative Unique Users). There is no unique-user count for an arbitrary window such as “the last 28 days”.

title: Average Daily Users
text:
Calculation
Average unique_users over the days in the window that have a row. Return the number of days present beside it, and quote the average only when that equals the number of days in the window. A missing day is a gap in the data, not a day with no users: dividing by the length of the window would count it as zero and pull the average down.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    AVG(CAST(unique_users AS DOUBLE)) AS average_daily_users,
    COUNT(DISTINCT CAST(from_date AS DATE)) AS days_present,
    -- the window's length, inclusive; quote the average only if they match
    date_diff('day', DATE '2026-09-03', DATE '2026-09-30') + 1 AS days_in_window
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_auth_total_logins
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-09-03' AND DATE '2026-09-30';


tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_auth_total_logins")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-09-03"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-09-30")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    average_daily_users = mean(as.double(unique_users), na.rm = TRUE),
    days_present = n_distinct(as.Date(from_date)),
    # the window's length, inclusive; quote the average only if they match
    days_in_window = !!(as.integer(as.Date("2026-09-30") - as.Date("2026-09-03")) + 1L)
  )

text:
Interpretation notes
Say “on a typical day” wherever it appears. Readers take “average users” for how many people use the service, which is a much larger number.
Comparing two windows. For a change against the previous window, use windows of the same length and check both are complete. Weekends run lower than weekdays, so a window should cover whole weeks: 28 days is four of each weekday.
The rate behind other metrics. Summing the same daily counts instead of averaging them gives user-days, the denominator of Calls per Active User.

title: Applications per Credential
text:
The average number of distinct applications a single credential reaches.
This metric measures how far the typical user spreads across CanadaLogin-integrated applications. It works because per-application unique_users counts each person once per application, while the CanadaLogin-wide count counts each person once overall: a user active on three applications adds three to the per-application sum but only one to the overall total. Dividing the two recovers the average number of applications per credential.
A value of 1.0 means the typical credential touches exactly one application; 2.0 means two, and so on.

title: Applications per Credential
Applications per Credential
text:
Interpretation notes
This is a population average, not a per-user count: a small group of power users spanning many applications can pull it up while most credentials stay on one.
The figure is inflated by internal applications, especially the migration app (GCS Migration Solution) and the profile management app (GC Sign In - Profile Management App). A user who reaches a single public service is still recorded as a unique user in the migration app when their credential is migrated from ECM, and in the profile management app when they manage their account, so they count two or three times in the per-application sum while counting once overall. To measure breadth across public-facing services, exclude the internal applications (listed at the top of this chapter) from the per-application sum.
Swap ytd_unique_users for mtd_unique_users to measure the same breadth over a different window.

title: Where Sessions Started
text:
Where readers came from when they opened a Signal Check or a dashboard: Slack, Teams, email, one of our own links, no link recorded, or another site.
The source belongs to the session, not the page. Google Analytics records where a session started, then credits every page in it. So “Slack, 20 sessions” on a page means 20 sessions that started from a Slack link and opened this page at some point. It does not mean 20 people clicked a Slack link to this page: a reader who came from Slack to a Signal Check and then followed a link to a dashboard counts as a Slack session on the dashboard too.

title: Where Sessions Started
text:
Calculation
From meta_page_traffic, sum sessions by page and source group over the reporting window. The groups map sessionsource:



Group
sessionsource




Slack
slack


Teams
teams, or anything starting teams.


Email
email


Our own links
latest-link, report_link, dashboard_link


No link recorded
(direct), (not set)


Other sites
anything else



The Readership dashboard’s source_group() holds the same map; change both together.
Our own links are the link to the latest Signal Check and the links inside a Signal Check or a dashboard. No link recorded is a bookmark, a typed address, or an app that drops the link’s source.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    pagepath_redacted,
    CASE
        WHEN sessionsource = 'slack' THEN 'Slack'
        WHEN sessionsource = 'teams' OR starts_with(sessionsource, 'teams.') THEN 'Teams'
        WHEN sessionsource = 'email' THEN 'Email'
        WHEN sessionsource IN ('latest-link', 'report_link', 'dashboard_link') THEN 'Our own links'
        WHEN sessionsource IN ('(direct)', '(not set)') THEN 'No link recorded'
        ELSE 'Other sites'
    END AS source_group,
    SUM(sessions) AS sessions
FROM google_analytics.meta_page_traffic
WHERE page_kind IN ('signal_check', 'dashboard')
  -- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  AND CAST(date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-09-01' AND DATE '2026-09-30'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY pagepath_redacted, sessions DESC, source_group;


tbl(con, in_schema("google_analytics", "meta_page_traffic")) |>
  filter(
    page_kind %in% c("signal_check", "dashboard"),
    # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
    as.Date(date) >= as.Date("2026-09-01"),
    as.Date(date) <= as.Date("2026-09-30")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    source_group = case_when(
      sessionsource == "slack" ~ "Slack",
      sessionsource == "teams" | substr(sessionsource, 1, 6) == "teams." ~ "Teams",
      sessionsource == "email" ~ "Email",
      sessionsource %in% c("latest-link", "report_link", "dashboard_link") ~ "Our own links",
      sessionsource %in% c("(direct)", "(not set)") ~ "No link recorded",
      TRUE ~ "Other sites"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(pagepath_redacted, source_group) |>
  summarise(sessions = sum(sessions, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(pagepath_redacted, desc(sessions), source_group)

title: Where Sessions Started
text:
Interpretation notes
Sessions add up within a page, not across pages. One session that opened two pages counts once on each, so the sessions on two pages together can exceed the sessions that reached either of them. For a whole product, sum per page and say “sessions that included a page”, or count each session once in the GA4 interface.
For a Signal Check, use its first 14 days. That is when the announcement posts send their readers. See Signal Check Views for the window.

title: Signal Check Views
text:
How many times each Signal Check was viewed in its first 14 days, and whether a new one is ahead of or behind a typical Signal Check at the same age.
Always name a Signal Check as “Signal Check #N”, never “edition” or a bare “#N”.

title: Signal Check Views
text:
Calculation
From meta_page_traffic, take the Signal Check pages: page_kind = 'signal_check' and a pagepath_redacted ending in <YYYYMMDD>_signal-check.html. The date in the file name is the day the Signal Check was sent.

Day 1 is the publication date. Views before it are the team reviewing the draft, so leave them out.
The first 14 days are the publication date and the 13 days after it. A fixed window makes Signal Checks comparable; views since publication favour the older ones.
Only Signal Checks published from 2026-07-23, when tracking began. Signal Check #1 and #2 came out before it and have no comparable figures.
The number comes from the page title, #N.

Typical Signal Check. To judge a new Signal Check that is, say, 5 days old, add up each earlier Signal Check’s views over its own first 5 days, and take the median. Use only Signal Checks with all 14 days tracked, and leave out the new one itself. Comparing at the same age is the point: a 5-day-old Signal Check against the others’ full 14 days always looks behind.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


WITH pages AS (
    SELECT
        pagepath_redacted,
        CAST(date AS DATE) AS day,
        -- the date in the file name is the day it was sent
        CAST(date_parse(regexp_extract(pagepath_redacted, '([0-9]{8})_signal-check', 1), '%Y%m%d') AS DATE)
            AS published,
        CAST(regexp_extract(pagetitle, '#([0-9]+)', 1) AS INTEGER) AS number,
        screenpageviews
    FROM google_analytics.meta_page_traffic
    WHERE page_kind = 'signal_check'
      AND regexp_like(pagepath_redacted, '[0-9]{8}_signal-check[.]html$')
)

SELECT
    MAX(number) AS signal_check,
    published,
    -- day 1 is the publication date; earlier views are the draft being reviewed
    SUM(screenpageviews) FILTER (WHERE day BETWEEN published AND date_add('day', 13, published))
        AS views_first_14_days,
    SUM(screenpageviews) FILTER (WHERE day >= published) AS views_since_published
FROM pages
-- tracking began on 2026-07-23
WHERE published >= DATE '2026-07-23'
GROUP BY pagepath_redacted, published
ORDER BY published;


tbl(con, in_schema("google_analytics", "meta_page_traffic")) |>
  filter(
    page_kind == "signal_check",
    str_detect(pagepath_redacted, "[0-9]{8}_signal-check[.]html$")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    day = as.Date(date),
    # the date in the file name is the day it was sent
    published = sql("CAST(date_parse(regexp_extract(pagepath_redacted, '([0-9]{8})_signal-check', 1), '%Y%m%d') AS DATE)"),
    number = sql("CAST(regexp_extract(pagetitle, '#([0-9]+)', 1) AS INTEGER)")
  ) |>
  # tracking began on 2026-07-23
  filter(published >= as.Date("2026-07-23")) |>
  group_by(pagepath_redacted, published) |>
  summarise(
    signal_check = max(number, na.rm = TRUE),
    # day 1 is the publication date; earlier views are the draft being reviewed
    views_first_14_days = sum(
      if_else(day >= published & day <= sql("date_add('day', 13, published)"), screenpageviews, 0L),
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    views_since_published = sum(if_else(day >= published, screenpageviews, 0L), na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  select(signal_check, published, views_first_14_days, views_since_published) |>
  arrange(published)

Views, not readers. A reader who opens a Signal Check twice counts twice. For how far readers get, see Dwell Time.
A young Signal Check is incomplete. Until its 14th day has been exported, views_first_14_days is still growing. Compare it with a typical Signal Check at the same age, not with the others’ 14-day totals.
Views come in early. Most of a Signal Check’s views land in the first few days, after it is announced, so a slow first day matters more than a slow tenth.

title: Service Level (Answered Within 60s)
text:
The proportion of calls answered within 60 seconds.
This metric is a standard call centre service-level measure of how quickly the queue is cleared. The source data stores only the weekly proportion (pct_answered_within_60s), not the underlying within-60s count, so combine weeks with a weighted average rather than re-deriving from counts.

title: Service Level (Answered Within 60s)
text:
Calculation
Calculate a weighted average of pct_answered_within_60s, weighted by calls_answered.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    SUM(
        CAST(pct_answered_within_60s AS DOUBLE)
        * CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE)
    )
    / NULLIF(SUM(CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE)), 0) AS service_level_60s
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
WHERE CAST(date_range_start AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-31';


tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date_range_start) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date_range_start) <= as.Date("2026-05-31")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    service_level_60s =
      sum(pct_answered_within_60s * calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

title: Service Level (Answered Within 60s)
text:
Interpretation notes
The result is a proportion between 0 and 1. Because only the weekly proportion is stored, the weighted average is an approximation of the true within-60s rate, but it is far closer than a simple average of weekly values.
Includes test calls. The weekly report gives the number of test calls, not their wait, so they cannot be taken out of the share.

title: Calls per Active User
text:
Call centre volume divided by the size of the active user base, so you can compare support demand across weeks even as the user base grows.
Raw call volume moves partly because the number of people using CanadaLogin changes. Normalizing by active users takes that out and leaves how often a typical user needed to phone in on a given day. The figure is scaled to calls per 100 active users to keep it in a readable range.

title: Calls per Active User
text:
Calculation
For each call centre reporting week, take calls_accepted from call_centre.weekly_activity_report, subtract that week’s test_calls, and divide by the total user-days in that week, then multiply by 100. User-days is the sum of ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_auth_total_logins.unique_users over the days whose date falls inside the week’s date_range_start to date_range_end, so the numerator and the denominator cover the same span of days. A weekly call count over weekly user-days is a per-day rate. The two tables store their dates as text, so both sides of the join are cast to DATE.
Use calls_accepted, not calls_answered: accepted counts everything that reached the queue, so an abandoned call still counts as demand. test_calls is a subset of accepted and is large enough at current volumes to be worth subtracting.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    w.date_range_start,
    w.date_range_end,
    CAST(w.calls_accepted AS BIGINT) AS calls_accepted,
    CAST(COALESCE(w.test_calls, 0) AS BIGINT) AS test_calls,
    CAST(w.calls_accepted - COALESCE(w.test_calls, 0) AS BIGINT) AS calls_excl_test,
    AVG(a.unique_users) AS avg_daily_active_users,
    CAST(w.calls_accepted - COALESCE(w.test_calls, 0) AS DOUBLE)
        / SUM(a.unique_users) * 100 AS calls_per_100_dau
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report AS w
JOIN ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_auth_total_logins AS a
    ON CAST(a.date AS DATE)
       BETWEEN CAST(w.date_range_start AS DATE) AND CAST(w.date_range_end AS DATE)
GROUP BY w.date_range_start, w.date_range_end, w.calls_accepted, w.test_calls
ORDER BY w.date_range_start;


weekly <- tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  select(date_range_start, date_range_end, calls_accepted, test_calls)

dau <- tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_auth_total_logins")) |>
  select(dau_date = date, unique_users)

weekly |>
  cross_join(dau) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(dau_date) >= as.Date(date_range_start),
    as.Date(dau_date) <= as.Date(date_range_end)
  ) |>
  group_by(date_range_start, date_range_end, calls_accepted, test_calls) |>
  summarise(
    avg_daily_active_users = mean(unique_users, na.rm = TRUE),
    user_days = sum(unique_users, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    test_calls = coalesce(test_calls, 0),
    calls_excl_test = calls_accepted - test_calls,
    calls_per_100_dau = calls_excl_test / user_days * 100
  ) |>
  arrange(date_range_start) |>
  select(
    date_range_start,
    date_range_end,
    calls_accepted,
    test_calls,
    calls_excl_test,
    avg_daily_active_users,
    calls_per_100_dau
  )

title: Calls per Active User
text:
Interpretation notes
Both sides are per-day averages over the same Sunday to Saturday week: average daily calls over average daily active users. On a typical day, roughly this many calls came in per 100 active users. This converts cleanly to a percentage, e.g., 2 calls per 100 users means 2% of users called on a given day.
Watch the units. Dividing a whole week of calls by one day’s active users reads about seven times too high. Normalizing by user-days avoids that and holds up for a partial week, since the day count comes from the data rather than a hardcoded 7. avg_daily_active_users is output for auditing only; the rate comes from the sum.
A call centre week runs Sunday to Saturday, from the report’s own date_range_start and date_range_end. The IBM Verify metrics anchor weeks on Monday, so the two do not line up; the join and the denominator follow the call centre boundaries.
A week appears only once daily active user data exists for it, so the series starts near the April 22, 2026 launch.

title: Call Topic Share
text:
Calculation
Count records by cleaned topic, then divide each topic count by the total count across all topics.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


WITH topic_counts AS (
    SELECT
        REGEXP_REPLACE(TRIM(statobject), '\s+', ' ') AS call_topic,
        COUNT(*) AS topic_count
    FROM call_centre.weekly_topic_dump
    GROUP BY REGEXP_REPLACE(TRIM(statobject), '\s+', ' ')
)

SELECT
    call_topic,
    topic_count,
    CAST(topic_count AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(topic_count) OVER (), 0) AS topic_share
FROM topic_counts
ORDER BY topic_count DESC;


tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_topic_dump")) |>
  mutate(
    call_topic = str_squish(statobject)
  ) |>
  count(call_topic, name = "topic_count") |>
  mutate(
    topic_share = as.double(topic_count) / sum(topic_count, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(topic_count))

title: Call Topic Share
text:
Interpretation notes
Topic share is useful for comparing relative demand across contact reasons. Interpret alongside total call volume.
This is a share of topic records, not of callers. A call can carry several topics, so a call counts once per topic here. For the share of callers who asked about a topic, see Calls by Topic Category.

title: Average Handle Time
text:
The average total time agents spend per call, including any after-call wrap-up.
avg_handle_time_seconds covers more than avg_call_length_seconds: it adds wrap-up work after the caller disconnects. Like the other averages, combine weeks with a weighted mean.

title: Average Handle Time
text:
Calculation
Calculate a weighted average of avg_handle_time_seconds, weighted by calls_answered.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    SUM(
        CAST(avg_handle_time_seconds AS DOUBLE)
        * CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE)
    )
    / NULLIF(SUM(CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE)), 0) AS weighted_avg_handle_time_seconds
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
WHERE CAST(date_range_start AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-31';


tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date_range_start) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date_range_start) <= as.Date("2026-05-31")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    weighted_avg_handle_time_seconds =
      sum(avg_handle_time_seconds * calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

title: Average Handle Time
text:
Interpretation notes
Average handle time is always at least as large as average call length. A widening gap between the two points to growing after-call work.
Includes test calls. The weekly report gives the number of test calls, not their handle time, so they cannot be taken out of the average.

title: Average Call Length
text:
The average length of answered calls.
The overall average call length is calculated as a weighted mean of avg_call_length_seconds, weighted by calls_answered. This is preferable to a simple average of weekly averages because weeks with more answered calls should contribute more to the overall result.

title: Average Call Length
text:
Calculation
Calculate a weighted average of weekly average call length, weighted by the number of answered calls.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


Weighted average over a period:
SELECT
    SUM(
        CAST(avg_call_length_seconds AS DOUBLE)
        * CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE)
    )
    / NULLIF(SUM(CAST(calls_answered AS DOUBLE)), 0) AS weighted_avg_call_length_seconds
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
WHERE CAST(date_range_start AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-31';
By week:
SELECT
    date_range_start,
    date_range_end,
    CAST(avg_call_length_seconds AS DOUBLE) AS avg_call_length_seconds,
    CAST(calls_answered AS BIGINT) AS calls_answered
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
ORDER BY date_range_start;


Weighted average over a period:
tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date_range_start) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date_range_start) <= as.Date("2026-05-31")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    weighted_avg_call_length_seconds =
      sum(avg_call_length_seconds * calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(calls_answered, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
By week:
tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  arrange(date_range_start) |>
  select(
    date_range_start,
    date_range_end,
    avg_call_length_seconds,
    calls_answered
  )

title: Abandonment Rate
text:
The proportion of accepted calls that were abandoned before being answered.
This metric is useful for understanding how often callers give up while waiting. It is closely tied to wait times: rising delay often drives rising abandonment.

title: Abandonment Rate
text:
Calculation
Divide the sum of calls_abandoned by the sum of calls_accepted over the selected reporting period. Summing the raw counts gives a volume-weighted rate; do not average the weekly calls_abandoned_pct column.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    SUM(CAST(calls_abandoned AS DOUBLE))
        / NULLIF(SUM(CAST(calls_accepted AS DOUBLE)), 0) AS abandonment_rate
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
WHERE CAST(date_range_start AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-31';


tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date_range_start) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date_range_start) <= as.Date("2026-05-31")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    abandonment_rate =
      sum(calls_abandoned, na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(calls_accepted, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

title: Abandonment Rate
text:
Interpretation notes
The rate is a proportion between 0 and 1. Read it together with average delay; a spike in abandonment usually coincides with longer waits.
Includes test calls. The weekly report does not say which test calls were abandoned, so neither side of the rate can drop them consistently.

title: Platform
text:
Platform metrics for CanadaLogin, in the sre schema. It holds two groups of tables: incident tables, which record outages and how long they took to resolve, and uptime tables, which record whether each monitored site was up and how fast it responded.
The incident tables come from the CanadaLogin Platform team’s CanadaLogin_MTTR_Dashboard Google Sheet, maintained by hand in the CDS Google Drive. The sre-mttr-sheets-fetcher Lambda reads it through the Google Sheets API every Monday at 06:00 ET. Both tables have one row per incident and differ only in history: mttr_current holds the latest state of each incident, while mttr_history adds a dated snapshot of every incident on each upload.

Data quality
Because the source is a hand-maintained spreadsheet, a few caveats apply to both tables:

Timestamps are strings, not native timestamps. detected_at, acknowledged_at, mitigated_at, and resolved_at are text in America/Toronto local time at minute precision (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM). Parse them before doing date math. (fetched_at is a real timestamp, in UTC.)
URLs may carry trailing whitespace or embedded newlines. Trim slack_channel and postmortem_link before joining on or rendering them.
Categorical columns are unvalidated free text. severity, service, component, and root_cause_category are typed by hand, so expect occasional typos, casing, and spacing drift. The values listed in each field table are those observed so far, not a closed set.
The duration columns are rounded to the nearest minute from second-precision source times, so recomputing them from the displayed (minute-precision) timestamp strings can differ by up to a minute.

title: rp.alias
text:
Notes
Join on alias alone. Do not filter on source. source records where the name was first seen, not which system the name belongs to. Filtering by it before joining will silently drop matches for any alias that turns up in both systems.
One service, several aliases. A service has as many rows here as it has names. For example, MyCGC is MyCGC in Google Analytics but both MyCGC - CGC - .NET - Prod and MyCGC - CGC - Power Pages - Prod in IBM Verify. Joining a fact table through this lookup is a many-to-one join, so aggregate after the join, not before.
Not every string in the analytics tables is an alias. The rp_name breakdown in the Google Analytics funnel tables also contains RESERVED_TOTAL (the all-services rollup), (not set), and the empty string. None of these are services, and an inner join drops them. If you are reconciling totals, exclude RESERVED_TOTAL explicitly rather than relying on the join to remove it.
Aliases are exact strings, not patterns. They are matched literally, with no trimming or case folding. A new application name in IBM Verify will not resolve until it is added to the source sheet by hand.

title: ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_mfa_activity
text:
Notes
OTP factors log a “sent” event too. sms_otp, email_otp, and voice_otp log “sent” when the code goes out, then “success” or “failure” for each attempt. A mistyped code followed by the right one gives one “sent”, one “failure”, and one “success”. fido2 logs only “success” or “failure”.

For success rates, divide “success” by “success” plus “failure”, and exclude “sent”.
For usage, count “sent” for OTP factors and “success” plus “failure” for the others. Summing “sent” alone drops fido2.

Most email_otp is sign-up, not sign-in. The email check during sign-up logs an email_otp with no user, because the account does not exist yet. These are most email_otp “sent” events. The rest carry a user, and are most likely the same check when an existing user changes their email address. See mfa_activity in the raw stream.

title: IBM Verify Events
text:
Users
The user ID is subject in authentication_activity and mfa_activity, and userid in application_usage and adaptive_access. Both hold the same HMAC-SHA256 digest of the IBM Verify user ID, so they join across tables and stay stable over time. Count users as distinct values of it.
Exclude null, "", and the literal "UNKNOWN". IBM Verify logs "UNKNOWN" when it cannot tie an event to an account, such as a password attempt on a username that does not exist. The summary tables keep it and count it as one user, to match IBM’s own figures.
username, origin (the client IP address), and mfadevice are hashed the same way. Countries and regions are not hashed.

title: IBM Verify Events
text:
Time and partitions
time is a UTC string, for example 2026-09-15 00:00:05 UTC. The partition columns year, month, and day are strings for the UTC day.
Always filter on the partitions, which lets Athena skip every other day. Filtering only on time reads the whole table.
Reports use ET days, which end at 04:00 or 05:00 UTC. Read the following UTC day too, then convert:
date(with_timezone(CAST(substr(time, 1, 19) AS timestamp), 'UTC') AT TIME ZONE 'America/Toronto')
Distinct-user counts do not add up across days. See Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up.

title: ibm_verify.auth_total_logins
text:
Notes
unique_users, failed_logins, and successful_logins are daily values. The mtd_, ytd_, and rolling_365d_ unique-user fields are cumulative and should not be summed across rows; take the latest value within the window instead.
rolling_365d_unique_users is null before 2026-06-13, its implementation date.






Warning



ytd_unique_users and rolling_365d_unique_users may be unreliable. Both are computed by IBM Verify over a longer window than its underlying data retention actually covers, so the figures can undercount, and ytd_unique_users has been seen decreasing from one day to the next. Treat both as estimates only. See Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up for detail.


When a user signs in to CanadaLogin itself, IBM Verify records each authentication method as a separate event. Entering a username and password followed by a second factor like an OTP counts as two successful events. A mistyped password that is then entered correctly, followed by a correct OTP, counts as three events: two successful and one failed. Both successful_logins and failed_logins are therefore inflated relative to the number of distinct sign-in sessions.
This inflation applies only to signing in to CanadaLogin itself. Reaching an integrated application does not add to these counts at all: it raises an SSO event on app_login_counts instead. CanadaLogin uses the session the person already holds and issues the application a freshly minted assertion or token, so the person enters no password and no second factor.
Summing successful_logins is therefore a misleading indicator of actual user engagement. Instead, use the unique_users field, which is daily active users, and is a measure of the number of users who engaged with the system in a given day.

Notes
Keep both pagetitle and pagepath in mind when joining or filtering. Title alone is an unstable key: a page retitled in a release starts a fresh row with no link to its history (this has happened repeatedly to CanadaLogin’s sign-in and sign-up pages - see the task success rate metric for the concrete impact). title: google_analytics.funnels
text:
Notes
A funnel’s step names, order and population can change between versions - always check GitHub, not a memory of a prior version. Every CanadaLogin funnel has already had at least one step renamed or re-scoped since it was first defined (see the task success rate metric for a worked example). funnel_version exists so old and new definitions coexist rather than silently overwriting each other: always pin funnel_version in a query, or use the funnels_current view, which resolves the newest version per date automatically. Summing or averaging across versions blends two different definitions of the funnel into one meaningless number.
RESERVED_TOTAL is a real GA4 sentinel, not a relying party. A funnel breakdown caps at 15 distinct values; RESERVED_TOTAL is GA4’s grand total across all relying parties, including any beyond that cap, and is the correct number to read as the funnel’s overall rate.
window_incomplete rows are written, not dropped, and must be excluded from a trend. A window that reaches earlier than a funnel’s valid_from (or later than valid_to) is trimmed and flagged rather than skipped, so a scheduled job keeps running as a tagging boundary recedes.
activeusers is de-duplicated within its own window and is not additive across windows. Summing seven daily (window_days = "1") rows for a week, for example, is not the same query as one window_days = "7" row for that week - repeat users within the week are counted once by the 7-day row and once per day they appeared by the daily rows. Never sum activeusers across rows with different window_end or window_days values.

title: Google Analytics
text:
Export lag
All four tables are pulled with a deliberate two-day lag - the nightly sweep that runs the morning of August 5, 2026 lands a window ending August 3, 2026, not August 4, because GA4 takes 24 to 48 hours to finish processing a day’s events. Each day is written once and never re-pulled, so a window read too early would stay artificially low forever.
Two of these tables - funnels and funnel_metrics - are defined by version-controlled YAML rather than a fixed schema. For what a funnel step or a derived metric actually measures, the YAML on GitHub is the single canonical source, not this catalog: steps get renamed, re-scoped, or added as CanadaLogin’s own pages change, and the table pages describe the table shape rather than the current step names. See funnel_src/funnels/ in the pipeline repo.

Notes
Use error_code, not error or error_id. Some pages report one or the other, and a few rare circumstances report both. This is an open defect. Error code is calculated as:

error_id if its not (not set) and not blank
otherwise the first word of error if its not (not set) and not blank
otherwise the row is dropped

Code columns are strings. This means that leading zeros should not be dropped, but an open open defect remains where they are coerced to ints at some point upstream. This means that the error code “000” is sometimes reported as 000 and sometimes as 0.

title: google_analytics.funnel_metrics_current
text:
A view over funnel_metrics that resolves the current funnel_version automatically, the same way funnels_current does for funnels. Query this instead of funnel_metrics directly unless a specific past version is genuinely what’s wanted.
Each row is the same as a funnel_metrics row, restricted to the newest funnel_version available for that row’s (funnel_id, window_days, window_end).
Keywords: Google Analytics, GA4, funnel, task success, funnel version, current version

title: google_analytics.funnel_metrics_current
text:
Definition
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW funnel_metrics_current AS
WITH latest_per_date AS (
  SELECT funnel_id, window_days, window_end,
         MAX(CAST(funnel_version AS integer)) AS current_version
  FROM funnel_metrics
  GROUP BY funnel_id, window_days, window_end
)
SELECT f.*
FROM funnel_metrics f
JOIN latest_per_date d
  ON  f.funnel_id   = d.funnel_id
  AND f.window_days = d.window_days
  AND f.window_end  = d.window_end
  AND CAST(f.funnel_version AS integer) = d.current_version;
