title: google_analytics.funnels_current
text:
Notes
The partition keys are still typed string in the view’s output, the same as the base table - MAX(funnel_version) on the view still sorts lexically wrong if you ignore that the view has already picked one version per row. Query it the same way you’d query funnels: filter with quoted string literals (WHERE window_days = '7', not = 7), and don’t re-aggregate across funnel_version since the view has already resolved it.
Resolution is per (funnel_id, window_days, window_end), not a global max per funnel. If a funnel bumps from version 1 to version 2 partway through its history, dates before the bump still resolve to version 1 (version 2 was never run for them) and dates from the bump onward resolve to version 2 - one continuous time series, not a series that vanishes before the bump. This only holds because versions of the same funnel are assumed to measure the same underlying thing; it would not be a safe pattern for two versions that represent genuinely different metrics.

title: google_analytics.meta_page_traffic
text:
Notes
Filter and group on pagepath_redacted, never on pagepath. Signal Check pages are served at a path that includes a private token, so the links can’t be guessed. pagepath_redacted drops it.
Use page_kind to pick pages. It is derived from pagepath_redacted, and the first matching rule wins:

signal_check: a Signal Check edition (/r/YYYYMMDD_signal-check.html)
redirect: a redirect page that forwards to the latest edition. These are listed by name in the pipeline’s ETL job
preview: a Cookbook PR preview (/canadalogin-metrics-cookbook/pr-preview/). These are the team’s own review views, not readership
cookbook: any other Cookbook page
dashboard: any other .html page under the publishing site’s /r/. This is a catch-all, so a new dashboard needs no code change. A new one-off page there would also count as a dashboard
other: anything else, including (unrecognized) paths

totalusers and newusers do not sum across rows. A reader who came from two sources, or saw two pages, is counted in both rows. This table can’t give an exact count of unique readers of an edition. sessions and screenpageviews are safe to sum. The reason is the same as why we can’t sum unique users in IBM Verify.

title: ibm_verify.app_login_counts
text:
Notes
total_logins, unique_users, failed_logins, and successful_logins are daily values. mtd_unique_users, ytd_unique_users, and rolling_365d_unique_users are cumulative counts of distinct users and should not be summed across rows; take the latest value within the window instead.
rolling_365d_unique_users is null before 2026-06-13, its implementation date.






Warning



ytd_unique_users and rolling_365d_unique_users may be unreliable. Both are computed by IBM Verify over a longer window than its underlying data retention actually covers, so the figures can undercount, and ytd_unique_users has been seen decreasing from one day to the next. Treat both as estimates only. See Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up for detail.


Unlike auth_total_logins, these counts are not inflated by second factors. The per-authentication-method event inflation described there only happens when a person signs in to CanadaLogin itself. Reaching an integrated application uses the session they already hold: CanadaLogin issues the application a freshly minted assertion or token, the person enters no password or second factor, and one handoff records one SSO event. total_logins and successful_logins still count events rather than people, because one person can reach an application repeatedly. Use unique_users when the question is about how many distinct people used the application.

title: ibm_verify.mfa_activity
text:
Notes
Only OTP factor types (sms_otp, email_otp, voice_otp) generate a “sent” event, because they are issued before the user responds. Successfully clearing one of these challenges therefore counts as two events: first a “sent” event, then either a “success” or “failure” event depending on how the user responds. It is possible to generate multiple “success”/“failure” events on a single “sent” event if the user inputs their OTP incorrectly first and then correctly. Non-OTP factor types (fido2, kq, totp, ibm_verify_push) have no “sent” event and produce only “success”/“failure” rows.
When calculating MFA usage metrics, de-duplicate accordingly: count “sent” events for OTP factors (sending an email OTP but not using it is still usage), and “success”/“failure” events for non-OTP factors. Summing “sent” alone would silently drop every non-OTP factor.
When calculating success rate metrics, use the number of successful events divided by the sum of the success and failure events, excluding “sent”.

title: IBM Verify Counts
text:
Dates are strings
from_date and to_date are YYYY-MM-DD strings, not timestamps. Comparing them to a date fails with TYPE_MISMATCH, so cast first:
WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-09-01' AND DATE '2026-09-30'
In R, wrap both sides in as.Date(): filter(as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-09-01")). A bare string on the right fails the same way, because RAthena turns ISO-date strings into DATE literals.

title: jira.psom_sla
text:
Notes
The four SLAs.

first_response: Jira’s “Time to first response”.
time_to_done: Jira’s “Time to done”, for the whole ticket. It keeps running while the ticket is escalated and pauses while waiting for the customer.
pso_time_to_done: “Time to Done - PSO”, the PSO team’s touchtime. It pauses while the ticket is escalated, or waiting for the customer. It only started on tickets created from about 2026-08-06.
escalated_to_pt: “Escalated to PT”, which runs while the ticket is escalated to the authentication team.

Working time. Goals and elapsed time count working minutes on the SLA’s 09:00 to 17:00 calendar, not wall-clock minutes, so a 40-hour goal is one working week.
Goals vary by ticket. The goal on a clock varies by ticket (for time_to_done, 16, 24, 40 and 72 hours all occur). A breach means the ticket missed its own target. To compare speed across tickets, use elapsed_minutes rather than breached.
Which cycle. A Jira SLA can restart when a ticket is reopened. Each row describes the running cycle if there is one, otherwise the last completed cycle. Earlier cycles are not kept.
Backfilled history (through 2026-09-28). Snapshots are daily from 2026-09-29. Before that they were weekly, on Mondays, and were backfilled from the sla_* columns that psom used to carry. The older snapshots only carry first_response and time_to_done, and only due and breached. There are no rows for the other two SLAs, and goal_minutes, elapsed_minutes and paused are null. breached is null in every row of the 2026-06-30 and 2026-07-06 snapshots, which predate a pipeline fix. It is populated from 2026-07-07 on.

title: Relying Parties

Reference tables for identifying and grouping the services that use CanadaLogin, in the rp schema. They hold no measurements. They exist to give the analytics tables a shared service identifier, so that IBM Verify sign-in counts and Google Analytics funnel steps can be reported against the same list of services.
service holds one row per relying party, with its names, operator, and launch date. alias maps each of the many strings the source systems use for a service back to that service’s rp_id.
Both tables come from one hand-maintained Google Sheet, read every weekday by the rp-sync Lambda in cds-snc/canadalogin-reporting-data-pipeline. That pipeline owns the table structure. Do not change it from this side.

title: Relying Parties
text:
Joining through the lookup
Resolve a source-system name to a relying party by joining on alias, then join rp_id to service for the attributes:
SELECT s.service_name_en,
       sum(a.successful_logins) AS successful_logins
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_app_login_counts a
JOIN rp.alias al ON a.application_name = al.alias
JOIN rp.service s ON al.rp_id = s.rp_id
WHERE CAST(a.from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-07-01' AND DATE '2026-07-31'
GROUP BY s.service_name_en
Aggregate after the join, never before. Several IBM Verify application names can map to one service, so a pre-aggregated count keyed on application_name will split a service across its environments.

title: Relying Parties
text:
Data quality
Because the source is a hand-maintained spreadsheet, a few caveats apply to both tables:

The list is not a complete inventory. Services are added when they appear in IBM Verify or analytics data, so a live service with no traffic yet will be missing.
New names need a manual edit. An application name that appears in IBM Verify before someone adds it to the sheet will not resolve, and an inner join will drop its rows without complaint. Left join and check for nulls when you care about coverage.
Free-text columns are unvalidated. service_name_en, service_name_fr, and operator are typed by hand, so expect occasional drift in spelling and spacing. Group by gc_orgid rather than operator.
Neither table keeps history. Each refresh overwrites the previous one, so a service renamed in the sheet is renamed retroactively for every report.

text:
The proportion of accepted calls that were answered by an agent.
This metric is the complement of abandonment and any other non-answered outcomes. It summarizes how much of incoming demand the call centre actually served.

title: Answer Rate

Calculation
Divide the sum of calls_answered by the sum of calls_accepted over the selected reporting period.

        / NULLIF(SUM(CAST(calls_accepted AS DOUBLE)), 0) AS answer_rate
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report

The average delay before calls are answered.

title: Escalations to PSO
text: The number of calls the call centre escalated to Partner Success and Operations (PSO). The call centre calls these callbacks: the call passes to a higher level of support, which calls the person back.

title: Escalations to PSO
text:
Calculation
Count the distinct calls (call_no) in call_centre.weekly_topic_dump with a transactiontype of “Callback”, over a span of call dates. Every topic row of an escalated call carries the flag. The examples group by calendar month, but any span of call dates works.
Start no earlier than 2026-06-29, when escalation to PSO began. Callbacks before then were not handled the same way.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    date_trunc('month', call_date) AS month,
    COUNT(DISTINCT call_no) AS escalations
FROM call_centre.weekly_topic_dump
-- transactiontype is padded with trailing spaces
WHERE trim(transactiontype) = 'Callback'
  -- set the reporting window; escalation to PSO began on 2026-06-29
  AND call_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-07-01' AND DATE '2026-09-30'
GROUP BY date_trunc('month', call_date)
ORDER BY month;


tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_topic_dump")) |>
  filter(
    # transactiontype is padded with trailing spaces
    str_trim(transactiontype) == "Callback",
    # set the reporting window; escalation to PSO began on 2026-06-29
    call_date >= as.Date("2026-07-01"),
    call_date <= as.Date("2026-09-30")
  ) |>
  group_by(month = floor_date(call_date, "month")) |>

title: Escalations to PSO
text:
Interpretation notes
Escalations are rare. One or two calls can double a month’s count, so compare over long spans and read the count next to the escalation rate.
PSOM tickets are a cross-check, not the source. Each escalation becomes a ticket on the PSOM Jira board (jira.psom), created the next working day. Match them with form_topic LIKE '%Escalated from Call Center%' OR lower(summary) LIKE '%canadalogin callback%', reading each ticket from its own latest snapshot. The summary match catches PSOM-140 and PSOM-147, two callback tickets with a blank form topic. The two sources agree call for call, but a ticket count can still differ from this one: a count on form topic alone misses the blank-topic tickets, and a count by ticket creation date includes escalations whose calls are not yet in the call centre data.
The callback column in weekly_activity_report holds the same count by Sunday-to-Saturday week. It has no call dates, so it cannot give calendar months.

title: Calls Accepted
text:
The number of calls accepted by the call centre during a reporting period, not counting the test calls staff make to check the line.
This metric is useful for tracking call centre demand and understanding how contact volume changes over time.

title: Calls Accepted
text:
Calculation
Subtract test_calls from calls_accepted by reporting period, or sum the difference across periods for a total. A missing test_calls means none were made, so read it as 0. Test calls are a subset of accepted calls, and at current volumes they are large enough to matter.

By week:
SELECT
    date_range_start,
    date_range_end,
    CAST(calls_accepted AS BIGINT) AS calls_accepted,
    CAST(COALESCE(test_calls, 0) AS BIGINT) AS test_calls,
    -- a missing test_calls means none were made
    CAST(calls_accepted - COALESCE(test_calls, 0) AS BIGINT) AS calls
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
ORDER BY date_range_start;
Total over a period:
SELECT
    SUM(CAST(calls_accepted - COALESCE(test_calls, 0) AS BIGINT)) AS total_calls
FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
WHERE CAST(date_range_start AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-31';


By week:
tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>

    date_range_start,
    date_range_end,

Test calls are left out by default across the call centre recipes. Only this count can drop them: the weekly report gives the number of test calls, not their waits, lengths, or outcomes. The recipes built on answered or abandoned calls, and the averages, say that they include them. The topic dump has no test calls.

title: Calls by Topic Category
text:
How many calls were about each topic, and what share of all calls that is. Grouped into categories, this answers “what share of callers asked about X”.
It is a different measure from Call Topic Share, which answers “what share of the conversation was about X”. An agent can log several topics on one call. Call Topic Share counts topic records, so a call counts once per topic and the shares add up to 100%. This metric counts calls, so a call counts once per topic it touched, and the shares add up to more than 100%. Say which one a figure is: the two can differ by more than a factor of two for the same topic.

title: Calls by Topic Category
text:
Calculation
Pick whole weeks of the weekly activity report (Sunday to Saturday). Take the topic records whose call_date falls inside those weeks, clean each topic, and count distinct call_no per topic. Divide by the weeks’ calls, excluding test calls (see Calls Accepted).
The denominator is the weekly report rather than the calls in the topic dump, because some calls have no topic logged. Every call is a caller; a call with no topic is a caller whose reason was not recorded.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


WITH weeks AS (
    SELECT
        CAST(date_range_start AS DATE) AS week_start,
        CAST(date_range_end AS DATE) AS week_end,
        -- calls excluding test calls; a missing test_calls means none
        calls_accepted - COALESCE(test_calls, 0) AS calls
    FROM call_centre.weekly_activity_report
    -- set the reporting window in whole weeks
    WHERE CAST(date_range_start AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-09-06' AND DATE '2026-09-27'
),
topics AS (
    -- one row per call and topic, so a topic logged twice on a call counts once
    SELECT DISTINCT
        call_no,
        REGEXP_REPLACE(TRIM(statobject), '\s+', ' ') AS call_topic
    FROM call_centre.weekly_topic_dump
    WHERE call_date BETWEEN (SELECT MIN(week_start) FROM weeks)
                        AND (SELECT MAX(week_end) FROM weeks)
)

SELECT
    call_topic,
    COUNT(*) AS calls,
    CAST(COUNT(*) AS DOUBLE) / (SELECT SUM(calls) FROM weeks) AS share_of_calls
FROM topics
GROUP BY call_topic
ORDER BY calls DESC, call_topic;


weeks <- tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_activity_report")) |>
  # set the reporting window in whole weeks
  filter(
    as.Date(date_range_start) >= as.Date("2026-09-06"),
    as.Date(date_range_start) <= as.Date("2026-09-27")
  ) |>
  transmute(
    week_start = as.Date(date_range_start),
    week_end = as.Date(date_range_end),
    # calls excluding test calls; a missing test_calls means none
    calls = calls_accepted - coalesce(test_calls, 0)
  ) |>
  collect()

tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_topic_dump")) |>
  filter(
    call_date >= !!min(weeks$week_start),
    call_date <= !!max(weeks$week_end)
  ) |>
  # one row per call and topic, so a topic logged twice on a call counts once
  distinct(call_no, call_topic = str_squish(statobject)) |>
  count(call_topic, name = "calls") |>
  mutate(share_of_calls = as.double(calls) / !!sum(weeks$calls)) |>
  arrange(desc(calls), call_topic)

The windows have to match. The weekly report runs Sunday to Saturday. Cut the topic records to the same days, or a topic’s calls and the calls under it cover different spans.

title: Escalation Rate
text:
Calculation
Divide the escalations by the distinct calls (call_no) in call_centre.weekly_topic_dump over the same span of call dates. Both come from the same table, so they cover the same calls. The examples group by calendar month, but any span of call dates works.

    date_trunc('month', call_date) AS month,
    COUNT(DISTINCT call_no) AS calls,
    -- transactiontype is padded with trailing spaces
    COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN trim(transactiontype) = 'Callback' THEN call_no END) AS escalations,
    CAST(COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN trim(transactiontype) = 'Callback' THEN call_no END) AS DOUBLE)
        / COUNT(DISTINCT call_no) AS escalation_rate
FROM call_centre.weekly_topic_dump
-- set the reporting window; escalation to PSO began on 2026-06-29
WHERE call_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-07-01' AND DATE '2026-09-30'
GROUP BY date_trunc('month', call_date)
ORDER BY month;


tbl(con, in_schema("call_centre", "weekly_topic_dump")) |>
  filter(
    # set the reporting window; escalation to PSO began on 2026-06-29
    call_date >= as.Date("2026-07-01"),
    call_date <= as.Date("2026-09-30")
  ) |>
  # transactiontype is padded with trailing spaces
  mutate(escalated_call = if_else(str_trim(transactiontype) == "Callback", call_no, NA)) |>
  group_by(month = floor_date(call_date, "month")) |>
  summarise(
    calls = n_distinct(call_no),
    escalations = n_distinct(escalated_call)

title: Escalation Rate
text:
Interpretation notes
The denominator is the topic dump, not the weekly report. The weekly report’s calls_accepted has no call dates, so it cannot be cut to the same span as the escalations, and it includes test calls. The topic dump has no test calls, but it misses calls with no topic logged, so it reads slightly below the weekly report. That pushes the rate up slightly.
One call moves the rate. Escalations are rare, so a single call can change a month’s rate by a percentage point or more. Show the counts next to the rate, and prefer longer spans.
A partial period is a rate to date. Label it with its last day of call centre data, and cut escalations and calls at that same day.

title: Top 10 Call Topics
text:
The ten most common call topics in the call centre topic data.
This is useful for quickly identifying the most common reasons people contact the call centre.

title: Top 10 Call Topics

Calculation
Count records by cleaned topic, calculate topic share, and return the top 10 by topic count.

    SELECT

        COUNT(*) AS topic_count
    FROM call_centre.weekly_topic_dump
    GROUP BY REGEXP_REPLACE(TRIM(statobject), '\s+', ' ')

topic_shares AS (
    SELECT
        call_topic,
        topic_count,
        CAST(topic_count AS DOUBLE)
            / NULLIF(SUM(topic_count) OVER (), 0) AS topic_share

SELECT

    topic_count,
    topic_share
FROM topic_shares
-- sort on topic_count desc, then call_topic asc to break ties deterministically
ORDER BY topic_count DESC, call_topic
LIMIT 10;

This is a share of topic records, not of callers. A call can carry several topics, so a call counts once per topic here. For the share of callers who asked about a topic, see Calls by Topic Category.

title: Dwell Time
text:
How long readers keep a Signal Check edition or a published dashboard open and visible, measured per page from the meta-analytics GA4 property.
Dwell time is a drop-off curve, not a single average. Each page fires one event the first time a page view reaches 1, 5, 15, 30, 60, 120, 300, and 600 seconds of visible time (read_1s through read_600s). The share of page views that reached each mark shows how far readers get. The median reader’s dwell time is read off that curve.
Only Signal Check editions and the dashboards fire these events. The Metrics Cookbook stream does not, nor does any production CanadaLogin page.

title: Dwell Time
text:
Calculation
Dwell curve: for each page and each milestone, divide the read_Ns event count by the page_view event count over the reporting window. Both come from meta_page_events.
Median dwell time: the time at which half of the page’s views were still open. Take the last milestone at least half the views reached and the next one, and interpolate on a log scale to where the share crosses 50%. It is 0 when fewer than half reached 1 second, and infinite when half were still open at 600 seconds.
Total reading time: count each page view as the last milestone it reached, and add them up. A view that reached 60 seconds but not 120 counts as 60 seconds, one that reached 600 counts as 600, and one that never reached 1 second counts as 0. From the event counts, that is each milestone times the views that reached it but not the next one, summed.
Group on pagepath_redacted, never pagepath, which holds a private token for Signal Check pages.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


Dwell curve:
WITH events AS (
    SELECT
        pagepath_redacted,
        eventname,
        SUM(eventcount) AS n
    FROM google_analytics.meta_page_events
    WHERE page_kind IN ('signal_check', 'dashboard')
      AND (eventname = 'page_view' OR REGEXP_LIKE(eventname, '^read_[0-9]+s$'))
      -- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
      AND CAST(date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-09-01' AND DATE '2026-09-30'
    GROUP BY pagepath_redacted, eventname
),
views AS (
    SELECT pagepath_redacted, n AS page_views
    FROM events
    WHERE eventname = 'page_view'
)
SELECT
    e.pagepath_redacted,
    CAST(REGEXP_EXTRACT(e.eventname, '[0-9]+') AS INTEGER) AS milestone_seconds,
    v.page_views,
    e.n AS page_views_reached,
    CAST(e.n AS DOUBLE) / v.page_views AS share_reached
FROM events e
JOIN views v ON e.pagepath_redacted = v.pagepath_redacted
WHERE e.eventname <> 'page_view'
ORDER BY e.pagepath_redacted, milestone_seconds;
Median dwell time:
WITH events AS (
    SELECT
        pagepath_redacted,
        eventname,
        SUM(eventcount) AS n
    FROM google_analytics.meta_page_events
    WHERE page_kind IN ('signal_check', 'dashboard')
      AND (eventname = 'page_view' OR REGEXP_LIKE(eventname, '^read_[0-9]+s$'))
      -- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
      AND CAST(date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-09-01' AND DATE '2026-09-30'
    GROUP BY pagepath_redacted, eventname
),
views AS (
    SELECT pagepath_redacted, n AS page_views
    FROM events
    WHERE eventname = 'page_view'
),
-- every milestone, so one nobody reached reads as zero, not missing
curve AS (
    SELECT
        v.pagepath_redacted,
        v.page_views,
        m.seconds,
        CAST(COALESCE(e.n, 0) AS DOUBLE) / v.page_views AS share,
        LEAD(m.seconds) OVER (PARTITION BY v.pagepath_redacted ORDER BY m.seconds) AS next_seconds,
        LEAD(CAST(COALESCE(e.n, 0) AS DOUBLE) / v.page_views)
            OVER (PARTITION BY v.pagepath_redacted ORDER BY m.seconds) AS next_share
    FROM views v
    CROSS JOIN UNNEST(ARRAY[1, 5, 15, 30, 60, 120, 300, 600]) AS m (seconds)
    LEFT JOIN events e
        ON e.pagepath_redacted = v.pagepath_redacted
       AND e.eventname = 'read_' || CAST(m.seconds AS VARCHAR) || 's'
),
crossing AS (
    SELECT
        *,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY pagepath_redacted ORDER BY seconds DESC) AS rn
    FROM curve
    WHERE share >= 0.5
)
SELECT
    v.pagepath_redacted,
    v.page_views,
    CASE
        -- fewer than half of the page views reached 1 second
        WHEN c.seconds IS NULL THEN 0
        -- half were still open at the last milestone
        WHEN c.next_seconds IS NULL THEN infinity()
        ELSE exp(ln(c.seconds) + (c.share - 0.5) / (c.share - c.next_share)
                 * (ln(c.next_seconds) - ln(c.seconds)))
    END AS median_dwell_seconds
FROM views v
LEFT JOIN crossing c
    ON c.pagepath_redacted = v.pagepath_redacted
   AND c.rn = 1
ORDER BY v.pagepath_redacted;
Total reading time:
WITH events AS (
    SELECT
        pagepath_redacted,
        eventname,
        SUM(eventcount) AS n
    FROM google_analytics.meta_page_events
    WHERE page_kind IN ('signal_check', 'dashboard')
      AND (eventname = 'page_view' OR REGEXP_LIKE(eventname, '^read_[0-9]+s$'))
      -- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
      AND CAST(date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-09-01' AND DATE '2026-09-30'
    GROUP BY pagepath_redacted, eventname
),
reached AS (
    SELECT
        pagepath_redacted,
        CAST(REGEXP_EXTRACT(eventname, '[0-9]+') AS INTEGER) AS seconds,
        n
    FROM events
    WHERE eventname <> 'page_view'
),
stops AS (
    SELECT
        pagepath_redacted,
        seconds,
        -- views whose last milestone this was: reached it, not the next one
        GREATEST(n - COALESCE(LEAD(n) OVER (PARTITION BY pagepath_redacted ORDER BY seconds), 0), 0)
            AS stopped_here
    FROM reached
)
SELECT
    pagepath_redacted,
    SUM(seconds * stopped_here) AS reading_seconds
FROM stops
GROUP BY pagepath_redacted
ORDER BY pagepath_redacted;


Dwell curve:
events <- tbl(con, in_schema("google_analytics", "meta_page_events")) |>
  filter(
    page_kind %in% c("signal_check", "dashboard"),
    eventname == "page_view" | str_detect(eventname, "^read_[0-9]+s$"),
    # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
    as.Date(date) >= as.Date("2026-09-01"),
    as.Date(date) <= as.Date("2026-09-30")
  ) |>
  group_by(pagepath_redacted, eventname) |>
  summarise(n = sum(eventcount, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

views <- events |>
  filter(eventname == "page_view") |>
  select(pagepath_redacted, page_views = n)

events |>
  filter(eventname != "page_view") |>
  inner_join(views, by = "pagepath_redacted") |>
  transmute(
    pagepath_redacted,
    milestone_seconds = as.integer(str_extract(eventname, "[0-9]+")),
    page_views,
    page_views_reached = n,
    share_reached = as.numeric(n) / page_views
  ) |>
  arrange(pagepath_redacted, milestone_seconds)
Median dwell time:
milestones <- c(1, 5, 15, 30, 60, 120, 300, 600)

# The time half the page views were still open, interpolated on a log scale
# between the milestones either side of 50%. `seconds` must be sorted.
median_read <- function(seconds, share) {
  above <- which(share >= 0.5)
  if (length(above) == 0L) return(0)
  i <- max(above)
  if (i == length(seconds)) return(Inf)
  step <- (share[i] - 0.5) / (share[i] - share[i + 1L])
  exp(log(seconds[i]) + step * (log(seconds[i + 1L]) - log(seconds[i])))
}

title: Dwell Time
text:
Interpretation notes
Only visible time counts. The clock pauses while the tab is in the background and resumes when the reader comes back, so a tab left open overnight does not reach read_600s unless someone is looking at it.
The median is an estimate between two measured milestones. A median_dwell_seconds of 45 means half the views passed 30 seconds and fewer than half passed 60; the interpolation places the crossing in between. An infinite median means half the views were still open at 10 minutes, so report it as “over 10 minutes”. Signal Checks before #9 report the floor milestone instead, the longest milestone at least half the views reached, so their medians read lower.
To combine pages, such as every dashboard, add their page_view and read_Ns counts across the pages first, then build one curve and read the median off it. Never average the per-page medians: a page with five views would count as much as one with ninety.
Total reading time is a floor. Every view counts at the last milestone it passed, not at the time it was really open, so the total is time readers spent at the least. Say “at least” when you quote it. A view open for four minutes counts as two, and the 600-second cap means a long read counts as ten minutes.
Prefer the curve or the median to an average. Readership is small, often a few dozen page views per page per month, and one forgotten tab can move a mean a long way. At these counts, check page_views before comparing two pages. A share built on five page views is too unstable to rank.
The curve counts page views, not people. A reader who reloads the page, or comes back on another day, starts the milestones again and counts twice. Use page_views as the denominator, since totalusers in meta_page_events can’t be summed across days.
read_1s is approximate. The page checks the clock once a second, so read_1s means “1 to 2 seconds”. Milestones from 15 seconds up are not affected.
This metric covers only Signal Check editions and the dashboards. Public CanadaLogin pages do not fire read_Ns events. For time on those pages, use GA4’s built-in average engagement time, which is only available in the GA4 interface, not in the data lake.

title: Task Success Rate
text:
The proportion of users who started a given task in CanadaLogin and reached that task’s defined end point, measured from Google Analytics 4 funnel data.
This is a family of metrics, not a single number. Each funnel declares its own task success rate as a step_ratio in its YAML definition on GitHub. The entry and exit steps for each funnel are described below as of this writing, but the YAML is the canonical, versioned source - see funnel_src/funnels/ in the canadalogin-reporting-data-pipeline repo.
Only sign-up, password recovery and the two migration tasks end on a screen that confirms the task is done. Sign-in cannot, and the 2-step recovery exit is a later cleanup screen. See the task notes before comparing tasks or reading any one rate as a completion rate.

title: Task Success Rate
text:
Calculation
Each funnel’s task success rate is already computed and stored as one row per window in funnel_metrics: the exit step’s activeUsers divided by the entry step’s, for that funnel run. There is no ratio to compute by hand - filter to the funnel and metric, and read value. Query funnel_metrics_current rather than funnel_metrics directly, so a future funnel version bump can’t silently blend two definitions together. Filter breakdown_value = 'RESERVED_TOTAL' for the overall rate across all relying parties; substitute a specific relying party name for a per-RP figure. The funnels catalog entry explains the RESERVED_TOTAL and window_incomplete conventions.
For one task, set funnel_id to the value given in that task’s notes.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


One task:
SELECT
    window_end,
    value AS task_success_rate
FROM google_analytics.funnel_metrics_current
WHERE funnel_id = 'sign_in'
  AND metric_id = 'task_success'
  AND window_days = '7'
  AND breakdown_value = 'RESERVED_TOTAL'
  AND NOT window_incomplete
  -- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  AND CAST(window_end AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-07-14' AND DATE '2026-08-03'
ORDER BY window_end;
Every task:
SELECT
    funnel_id,
    window_end,
    value AS task_success_rate
FROM google_analytics.funnel_metrics_current
WHERE metric_id = 'task_success'
  AND window_days = '7'
  AND breakdown_value = 'RESERVED_TOTAL'
  AND NOT window_incomplete
  -- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  AND CAST(window_end AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-08-03' AND DATE '2026-08-31'
ORDER BY funnel_id, window_end;


One task:
tbl(con, in_schema("google_analytics", "funnel_metrics_current")) |>
  filter(
    funnel_id == "sign_in",
    metric_id == "task_success",
    window_days == "7",
    breakdown_value == "RESERVED_TOTAL",
    !window_incomplete,
    # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
    as.Date(window_end) >= as.Date("2026-07-14"),
    as.Date(window_end) <= as.Date("2026-08-03")
  ) |>
  select(window_end, task_success_rate = value) |>
  arrange(window_end)
Every task:
tbl(con, in_schema("google_analytics", "funnel_metrics_current")) |>
  filter(
    metric_id == "task_success",

title: Task Success Rate
text:
Interpretation notes
The queries above use window_days = '7', a rolling weekly rate recomputed nightly on a 7-day window ending each date. Three window lengths exist, and switching between them is a one-line change:

'1' is the same metric on a single day. It is the noisiest of the three, but it is the only one that shows the exact date something changed.
'7' is the usual default. Every window holds one of each weekday, so day-of-week effects wash out.
'28' is a rolling four-week window. It is the steadiest of the three and the one to use for monthly reporting.

Windows overlap, so consecutive rows are not independent. One unusual day shows up in 7 weekly rows and 28 monthly ones. A NULL rate means nobody reached the entry step in that window. These rows are rare. Drop them rather than counting them as 0.0, or an average will read too low.

Task notes

All tasks

Users, not attempts. Every step counts distinct activeUsers in the window. A user who fails, retries and succeeds counts once, as a success. A user who fails three times and gives up counts once, as a failure. The rate is a share of people, not of attempts.
Sign ups and sign ins without a valid destination RP are excluded. It is technically possible for someone to go through the sign up or sign in flow without entering via a valid RP service, via a link that specifies the CL manage app as the destination relying party. Actual users will always enter via a valid RP, so we can be confident that traffic with the Manage CanadaLogin RP id parameter represents internal employee traffic, rather than actul users. All funnels that are not manage app tasks therefore exclude traffic with the Manage App RP id parameter. Manage CanadaLogin app, which is internal. See Internal applications.
A series can change definition part way through. funnel_metrics_current returns the newest version for each date, and a new version is not always backfilled. Check funnel_version across the rows before reading a trend.



Sign in

Funnel ID: sign_in
Definition: sign_in.yaml
Entry: enter_email, the “Enter your email” screen
Exit: mfa_submit, pressing submit on the second-factor form

This rate measures submitting a second factor, but not necessarily success. The exit is pressing the submit button on the second-factor form. It is possible to submit an incorrect OTP code and count as a success in the task but fail to actually sign in. This is a limitation of what Google Analytics measures. This means the rate is marginally overstated, compared to a true sign-in success rate.
For an authentication success rate measured by IBM Verify itself, see Authentication Success Rate. It counts attempts rather than users and covers every sign-in, not only those that started in a tagged browser session, so the two numbers will not match.


Sign up

Funnel ID: sign_up
Definition: sign_up.yaml
Entry: terms, the Terms and Conditions screen
Exit: complete, the “Your CanadaLogin is complete” screen



Recover password

Funnel ID: recover_password
Definition: recover_password.yaml
Entry: reset_password, the “Reset your password” screen
Exit: complete, the “Your password has been reset” screen

Account checkers are excluded from version 5. Many people who start are checking whether they have an account, not recovering a password. They enter their email, enter the OTP code sent to them, and get error 26 (“This email is not associated with an account”). Counted as failures, they would make the rate mostly a measure of account checking. The funnel drops any user with a form_api_call_end event where error_id is 26 and form_id is passwordrecovery, using a GA4 user exclusion segment (the exclude_users block in the YAML). An excluded user leaves every step, not only the step where the error appeared.
The rate is a lower bound. Only the phone branch returns error 26. The passkey branch never looks up the email, and an address with no account fails the passkey prompt the same way a cancel does. Those checkers, and checkers who quit at the method choice screen, stay in and count as failures, even though they had no password to reset. The true success rate for account holders is higher.


Recover 2-step verification

Funnel ID: recover_2sv
Definition: recover_2sv.yaml
Entry: initiate_recovery, the “Initiate email verification” screen
Exit: confirmation, the “Delete sign-in methods you’re not using anymore” screen

Exit is a cleanup screen, not a confirmation. The last step is “Delete sign-in methods you’re not using anymore”, offered after a new method is set up.


Migration
Existing account:

Funnel ID: migration_existing_to_cl
Definition: migration_existing_to_cl.yaml
Entry: migration_not_skipped, answering the legacy sign-in prompt without skipping
Exit: migration_complete, the “Migration - Confirmation” screen

New account:

Funnel ID: migration_new_to_cl
Definition: migration_new_to_cl.yaml
Entry: migration_not_skipped, answering the legacy sign-in prompt without skipping
Exit: migration_complete, the “Migration - Confirmation” screen

The denominator is not the first step. In both funnels, task_success divides by migration_not_skipped, users who answered the legacy sign-in prompt without skipping it. The rate is the share of people who chose to link a legacy method and finished.
The prompt step has a time limit in migration_existing_to_cl. The legacy method prompt must follow the 2-step verification step within 30 minutes.

title: IBM Verify
text:
Metrics in this section come from IBM Verify, which records two different kinds of event. It raises an authentication event when someone presents an authentication method to CanadaLogin: a password, then a second factor. It raises an SSO event when someone who is already signed in reaches a partner service, and files that one under application usage. These are separate event types, so a figure taken from one is never comparable to a figure taken from the other.
A user signs in to CanadaLogin once and gets a session. Reaching a partner service afterwards does not sign them in again: CanadaLogin uses the session it already holds and issues the partner a freshly minted assertion or token. One sign-in, then as many handoffs as the user needs.
“Sign-in” is prose only. No table counts it, so it is never an output column name or an axis label, and names a metric only where that metric is labelled an estimate.
The relevant IBM Verify tables are:
Their from_date is a string, so every query below casts it. See Dates are strings.
Internal applications. Internal applications are typically excluded from public-facing adoption metrics. Which ones are internal comes from rp.service.is_internal, resolved to IBM Verify’s application names through rp.alias:
Use the subquery rather than a pasted list, so the classification stays in one place. See the internal applications note in notes.qmd.

That table has one row per day per MFA factor (mfa_type) per outcome (result), with the number of events in count. A sent row is a code issued; success and failure rows are outcomes. Most metrics here cover only the factors the public can sign in with.
IBM Verify files MFA as a subtype of the authentication event rather than as an event type of its own, so these counts are a slice of the CanadaLogin-wide authentication events, not a separate stream.

title: Average Daily SSO Events
text:
The average number of SSO events per day for each application over a selected reporting period.
This metric summarizes daily application usage into a single per-application average value. It is useful for understanding typical daily usage during a launch period, reporting window, or monitoring period.

title: Average Daily SSO Events
text:
Calculation
For each application, calculate the average of total_logins across all daily records in the selected reporting period.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    application_name,
    AVG(total_logins) AS average_daily_sso_events
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_app_login_counts
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-04-22' AND DATE '2026-05-31'
-- to exclude internal applications from adoption reporting, uncomment:
-- AND application_name NOT IN (
--     SELECT al.alias
--     FROM   rp.alias al
--     JOIN   rp.service s ON al.rp_id = s.rp_id
--     WHERE  s.is_internal
-- )
GROUP BY application_name
ORDER BY average_daily_sso_events DESC;


tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_app_login_counts")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-04-22"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-05-31")
  ) |>
  # to exclude internal applications from adoption reporting, uncomment:
  # anti_join(
  #   tbl(con, in_schema("rp", "alias")) |>
  #     inner_join(tbl(con, in_schema("rp", "service")), by = "rp_id") |>
  #     filter(is_internal) |>
  #     select(application_name = alias),
  #   by = "application_name"

  summarise(
    average_daily_sso_events = mean(total_logins, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(average_daily_sso_events))

The average is taken over the daily rows present for each application in the window, not over every calendar day. If an application has no row on a day with zero activity, that day does not pull the average down, so the figure reflects typical activity on active days.

title: Completed Sign-In Sessions (Estimated)
text: An estimate of the number of completed sign-in sessions to CanadaLogin over a selected reporting period, where a session is one user getting all the way through the sign-in flow regardless of how many authentication methods it took.

title: Completed Sign-In Sessions (Estimated)
text:
Calculation
A completed session has exactly one successful first-factor event (the password) plus zero or more successful second factors. Both kinds of success are lumped together in successful_logins on events_auth_total_logins, while the second-factor successes are counted separately on events_mfa_activity. Subtracting the second from the first leaves one event per session: the first-factor success. So sum successful_logins over the window and subtract the sum of mfa_activity.count where result = 'success', restricted to the factors that can complete a sign-in.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


WITH first_factor AS (
    SELECT SUM(successful_logins) AS successful_events
    FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_auth_total_logins
    -- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
    WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
),

second_factor AS (
    SELECT SUM(count) AS mfa_successes
    FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_mfa_activity
    -- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
    WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
      -- outcome events only; a "sent" OTP is an issuance, not a success
      AND result = 'success'
      -- email_otp validates an email address at sign-up and never enters
      -- successful_logins, so subtracting it would over-correct
      AND mfa_type IN ('sms_otp', 'voice_otp', 'fido2')
)

SELECT
    first_factor.successful_events - second_factor.mfa_successes
        AS estimated_completed_sessions
FROM first_factor
CROSS JOIN second_factor;


sign_in_types <- c("sms_otp", "voice_otp", "fido2")

successful_events <- tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_auth_total_logins")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-05-28")
  ) |>
  summarise(successful_events = sum(as.double(successful_logins), na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull(successful_events)

mfa_successes <- tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_mfa_activity")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-05-28"),
    # outcome events only; a "sent" OTP is an issuance, not a success
    result == "success",
    # email_otp validates an email address at sign-up and never enters
    # successful_logins, so subtracting it would over-correct
    mfa_type %in% sign_in_types
  ) |>
  summarise(mfa_successes = sum(as.double(count), na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull(mfa_successes)

The estimate works because each session contributes exactly one first-factor success no matter how many second factors it used:

email_otp is excluded because a successful email_otp does not increment successful_logins. It validates an email address at sign-up rather than completing a sign-in.
The estimate rests on two assumptions:

Passwordless and FIDO-first logins are undercounted. A session whose only factor is FIDO2 is one event in successful_logins and also a fido2 success in events_mfa_activity, so it nets to zero. The figure is therefore a slight underestimate.
The two tables are assumed to count sign-in second-factor successes the same way. Both derive from the same IBM Verify event stream, which makes this plausible, but it is not guaranteed by anything in the data catalog.

Because of these assumptions, label the result as estimated wherever it is reported, and never present it as an exact session count. title: Cumulative Unique Users
text:
The total number of distinct users who have signed in to CanadaLogin over a chosen reporting window: this month or this calendar year.
This metric is useful for understanding the overall reach and adoption of CanadaLogin over time. Note that it will not align with the sum of unique users across individual apps: a user who signs into App A and App B on the same day counts as two unique users at the app level but only one overall.

title: Cumulative Unique Users
text:
Calculation
Take the latest value of the cumulative unique-user column for the window of interest. The window is chosen by which column you read, not by a date filter (see the note on reporting timespans):

mtd_unique_users for month-to-date
ytd_unique_users for year-to-date

These columns are cumulative, so the most recent row holds the current total.

SELECT
    mtd_unique_users
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_auth_total_logins
ORDER BY from_date DESC
LIMIT 1;
Year-to-date:
SELECT
    ytd_unique_users
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_auth_total_logins
ORDER BY from_date DESC
LIMIT 1;

tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_auth_total_logins")) |>
  slice_max(
    from_date,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  pull(mtd_unique_users)

tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_auth_total_logins")) |>
  slice_max(
    from_date,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  pull(ytd_unique_users)

Interpretation notes
Each column resets on its own cadence: mtd_unique_users resets at the start of each month and ytd_unique_users at the start of each calendar year. Do not sum these columns across rows; they are already cumulative.
To compare a month in progress with the month before, read both on the same day of the month: the 12th against the 12th. If the earlier month is shorter, use its last day. Never compare a partial month with a finished one; the partial month always looks smaller.

title: MFA Challenges
text:
The number of second-factor challenges CanadaLogin issued at sign-in over a selected reporting period: one per code sent, and one per passkey prompt that reached an outcome.
This metric measures second-factor volume. It counts challenges, not people, and not outcomes: an SMS code that is sent and never entered is still a challenge. For the challenges that reached an outcome, see Second-factor Attempts.
It covers the factors the public can sign in with: sms_otp, voice_otp, and fido2 (passkeys). email_otp is left out because it only checks an email address at sign-up (see Sign-up Email Verification Rate), and kq, totp, qr, and ibm_verify_push are internal factors. For every factor the platform records, see All MFA Activity by Factor.

title: MFA Challenges
text:
Calculation
Restrict to the sign-in factors and sum count over the selected reporting period. The OTP factors (sms_otp, voice_otp) record both a sent event and a subsequent success/failure event for the same challenge; to avoid double-counting, only the sent row is used for these. fido2 does not generate a sent event, so its success/failure rows are used instead.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    SUM(count) AS mfa_challenges
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_mfa_activity
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
  -- the factors the public can sign in with; email_otp is a sign-up check
  AND mfa_type IN ('sms_otp', 'voice_otp', 'fido2')
  -- OTP types record both a "sent" event and a "success"/"failure" event for
  -- the same challenge. Counting all three would double-count them. fido2
  -- has no "sent" event and is counted through its outcome rows instead.
  AND (
    result = 'sent'
    OR (result IN ('success', 'failure') AND mfa_type = 'fido2')
  );


tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_mfa_activity")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-05-28"),
    # the factors the public can sign in with; email_otp is a sign-up check
    mfa_type %in% c("sms_otp", "voice_otp", "fido2"),
    # OTP types record both a "sent" and a "success"/"failure" event per
    # challenge; use only "sent" for these. fido2 has no "sent" event.
    result == "sent" |
      (result %in% c("success", "failure") & mfa_type == "fido2")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    mfa_challenges = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

text:
Interpretation notes
A challenge is not an attempt. Bot traffic that requests SMS codes it cannot read raises challenges without raising attempts, so a jump in challenges with no matching jump in Second-factor Attempts is a sign of automated traffic, not of more people signing in. Passkey (fido2) activity appears only from the 2026-07-06 rollout onward.

title: MFA Success Rate
text:
The proportion of second-factor attempts at sign-in that succeeded over a selected reporting period.
This metric is useful for monitoring how often users clear the second factor when they sign in. A falling rate can point to user friction with a particular factor, SMS delivery problems, or attack traffic.
It covers the factors the public can sign in with: sms_otp, voice_otp, and fido2 (passkeys). email_otp is not a second factor: it checks an email address at sign-up, and its rate is Sign-up Email Verification Rate. kq, totp, qr, and ibm_verify_push are internal factors. For one rate per factor, including those, see MFA Success Rate by Factor.

title: MFA Success Rate
text:
Calculation
Restrict to the sign-in factors. Divide the sum of count where result = 'success' by the sum of count where result is 'success' or 'failure'. OTP factor types also produce a 'sent' event per challenge, which must be excluded from both the numerator and the denominator, because sent rows do not represent outcomes.
To track the metric over time, bin the same calculation by week. Truncating from_date to the week groups each day into its Monday-anchored bin, so the result is one success rate per Monday-to-Sunday week.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


Overall:
SELECT
    CAST(SUM(count) FILTER (WHERE result = 'success') AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(count), 0) AS mfa_success_rate
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_mfa_activity
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
  -- the factors the public can sign in with; email_otp is a sign-up check
  AND mfa_type IN ('sms_otp', 'voice_otp', 'fido2')
  -- exclude "sent" rows; success rate is calculated from outcome events only.
  -- including "sent" would inflate the denominator and deflate the rate.
  AND result IN ('success', 'failure');
By week:
SELECT
    date_trunc('week', CAST(from_date AS DATE)) AS week_start,
    CAST(SUM(count) FILTER (WHERE result = 'success') AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(count), 0) AS mfa_success_rate
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_mfa_activity
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
  -- the factors the public can sign in with; email_otp is a sign-up check
  AND mfa_type IN ('sms_otp', 'voice_otp', 'fido2')
  -- exclude "sent" rows; success rate is calculated from outcome events only.
  -- including "sent" would inflate the denominator and deflate the rate.
  AND result IN ('success', 'failure')
-- date_trunc('week', ...) anchors each bin to its Monday
GROUP BY date_trunc('week', CAST(from_date AS DATE))
ORDER BY week_start;


Overall:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_mfa_activity")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-05-28"),
    # the factors the public can sign in with; email_otp is a sign-up check
    mfa_type %in% c("sms_otp", "voice_otp", "fido2"),
    # exclude "sent" rows; success rate is calculated from outcome events only.
    # including "sent" would inflate the denominator and deflate the rate.
    result %in% c("success", "failure")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    mfa_success_rate =
      sum(if_else(result == "success", as.double(count), 0), na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(count, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
By week:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_mfa_activity")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-05-28"),
    # the factors the public can sign in with; email_otp is a sign-up check
    mfa_type %in% c("sms_otp", "voice_otp", "fido2"),
    # exclude "sent" rows; success rate is calculated from outcome events only.
    # including "sent" would inflate the denominator and deflate the rate.
    result %in% c("success", "failure")
  ) |>
  # floor_date(..., "week") translates to Athena's date_trunc('week', ...),
  # which anchors each bin to its Monday
  mutate(week_start = floor_date(as.Date(from_date), "week")) |>
  group_by(week_start) |>
  summarise(
    mfa_success_rate =
      sum(if_else(result == "success", as.double(count), 0), na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(count, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(week_start)

In the weekly view, the first and last weeks of the reporting window are usually partial (the window rarely starts or ends on a Monday), so treat boundary weeks with caution when comparing trends.

title: Peak Daily Unique Users
text:
The highest number of unique users observed on any single day during the reporting period.
This metric is useful for identifying the maximum daily reach of an application and for understanding peak demand.

title: Peak Daily Unique Users
text:
Calculation
Take the maximum value of unique_users over the selected reporting period, grouped by application.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT
        application_name,
        from_date,
        unique_users,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY application_name
            ORDER BY unique_users DESC, from_date ASC
        ) AS rn
    FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_app_login_counts
    -- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
    WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
    -- to exclude internal applications from adoption reporting, uncomment:
    -- AND application_name NOT IN (
    --     SELECT al.alias
    --     FROM   rp.alias al
    --     JOIN   rp.service s ON al.rp_id = s.rp_id
    --     WHERE  s.is_internal
    -- )
)

SELECT
    application_name,
    from_date,
    unique_users AS peak_daily_unique_users
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY peak_daily_unique_users DESC;


tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_app_login_counts")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-05-28")
  ) |>
  # to exclude internal applications from adoption reporting, uncomment:
  # anti_join(
  #   tbl(con, in_schema("rp", "alias")) |>
  #     inner_join(tbl(con, in_schema("rp", "service")), by = "rp_id") |>
  #     filter(is_internal) |>
  #     select(application_name = alias),
  #   by = "application_name"
  # ) |>
  group_by(application_name) |>
  slice_max(
    unique_users,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  select(
    application_name,
    from_date,
    peak_daily_unique_users = unique_users
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(peak_daily_unique_users))

title: Sign-in Factor Share of Successes
text:
Each sign-in factor’s share of the second factors that succeeded over a selected reporting period. The fido2 row is the passkey share: of the people who cleared a second factor at sign-in, how many did it with a passkey.
This is the measure to use for passkey uptake. It compares like with like, a completed second factor against a completed second factor. The share in Sign-in MFA Activity by Factor does not: it counts an SMS code as soon as it is sent, entered or not, but a passkey only once the prompt reaches an outcome, so it understates passkeys.
It covers the factors the public can sign in with: sms_otp, voice_otp, and fido2. email_otp is a sign-up check, not a sign-in factor.

title: Sign-in Factor Share of Successes
text:
Calculation
Restrict to the sign-in factors and to result = 'success'. Sum count by mfa_type, then divide each factor’s successes by all sign-in successes.
For a trend, do the same per Monday-to-Sunday week, and leave off any week the reporting window cuts short: a part week has too few days to compare.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


By factor:
SELECT
    mfa_type,
    SUM(count) AS successes,
    CAST(SUM(count) AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(SUM(count)) OVER (), 0) AS share_of_successes
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_mfa_activity
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
  -- the factors the public can sign in with; email_otp is a sign-up check
  AND mfa_type IN ('sms_otp', 'voice_otp', 'fido2')
  AND result = 'success'
GROUP BY mfa_type
ORDER BY successes DESC;
Passkey share by week:
SELECT
    date_trunc('week', CAST(from_date AS DATE)) AS week_start,
    SUM(count) FILTER (WHERE mfa_type = 'fido2') AS passkey_successes,
    SUM(count) AS successes,
    CAST(SUM(count) FILTER (WHERE mfa_type = 'fido2') AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(count), 0) AS passkey_share
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_mfa_activity
-- whole Monday-to-Sunday weeks only: start on a Monday, end on a Sunday
WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-05' AND DATE '2026-05-24'
  AND mfa_type IN ('sms_otp', 'voice_otp', 'fido2')
  AND result = 'success'
-- date_trunc('week', ...) anchors each bin to its Monday
GROUP BY date_trunc('week', CAST(from_date AS DATE))
ORDER BY week_start;


By factor:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_mfa_activity")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-05-28"),
    # the factors the public can sign in with; email_otp is a sign-up check
    mfa_type %in% c("sms_otp", "voice_otp", "fido2"),
    result == "success"
  ) |>
  group_by(mfa_type) |>
  summarise(successes = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(
    share_of_successes =
      as.double(successes) / sum(successes, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(successes))
Passkey share by week:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_mfa_activity")) |>
  # whole Monday-to-Sunday weeks only: start on a Monday, end on a Sunday
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-01-05"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-05-24"),
    mfa_type %in% c("sms_otp", "voice_otp", "fido2"),
    result == "success"
  ) |>
  # floor_date(..., "week") translates to Athena's date_trunc('week', ...),
  # which anchors each bin to its Monday
  mutate(week_start = floor_date(as.Date(from_date), "week")) |>
  group_by(week_start) |>
  summarise(
    passkey_successes =
      sum(if_else(mfa_type == "fido2", count, 0L), na.rm = TRUE),
    successes = sum(count, na.rm = TRUE),
    passkey_share =
      sum(if_else(mfa_type == "fido2", as.double(count), 0), na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(count, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(week_start)

Passkeys (fido2) became generally available on 2026-07-06, so a window that starts earlier shows little or no passkey share. A share can rise because passkey use grew or because SMS use fell; read the share next to the successes behind it.

title: SSO Success Rate by Application
text:
The proportion of SSO events that succeeded, broken down by application.
This is the success rate of the handoff to an application, not of anyone signing in. It helps isolate problems to a specific application: one with a markedly lower success rate than its peers is worth investigating for integration or configuration issues.

title: SSO Success Rate by Application
text:
Calculation
Divide the sum of successful_logins by the sum of all attempts (successful_logins + failed_logins) over the selected reporting period, grouped by application.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    application_name,
    CAST(SUM(successful_logins) AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(successful_logins + failed_logins), 0) AS sso_success_rate
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_app_login_counts
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
-- optionally filter out internal applications; see the internal applications
-- note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  AND application_name NOT IN (
      SELECT al.alias
      FROM   rp.alias al
      JOIN   rp.service s ON al.rp_id = s.rp_id
      WHERE  s.is_internal
  )
GROUP BY application_name
ORDER BY sso_success_rate DESC;


internal_apps <- tbl(con, in_schema("rp", "alias")) |>
  inner_join(tbl(con, in_schema("rp", "service")), by = "rp_id") |>
  filter(is_internal) |>
  select(application_name = alias)

tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_app_login_counts")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-05-28")
  ) |>
  # optionally filter out internal applications; see the internal applications
  # note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  anti_join(internal_apps, by = "application_name") |>
  group_by(application_name) |>
  summarise(
    sso_success_rate =
      sum(as.double(successful_logins), na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(successful_logins + failed_logins, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(sso_success_rate))

text:
Interpretation notes
Compare applications against each other rather than against an absolute target. This measures the handoff to a relying party after the person has already signed in to CanadaLogin. The person enters no password and no second factor; the check is whether the session can be used for that application. It counts a different IBM Verify event type from the CanadaLogin-wide authentication success rate, so the two are not comparable.

title: SSO Events by Application
text:
The total number of SSO events recorded for each application over a selected time period.
IBM Verify raises an SSO event when someone who is already signed in reaches an application. It uses the CanadaLogin session they already hold, so the person enters no password and no second factor. This metric is useful for understanding usage volume across CanadaLogin-integrated applications. It counts events, not people: one person reaching an application several times contributes several events.
The source column is total_logins, but the event it counts is what IBM Verify calls an SSO event, part of application usage.

title: SSO Events by Application
SSO Events by Application
text:
Interpretation notes
This counts events, not people. Use this metric when the question is about system usage or activity volume. Use unique user metrics when the question is about reach.
These are a different IBM Verify event type from the CanadaLogin-wide authentication events, so never add the two together or present them side by side as comparable figures. Unlike the authentication events, SSO events are not inflated by second factors, because reaching an application uses the session the person already holds rather than asking them to authenticate again.

title: Authentication Events
text:
The total number of authentication events CanadaLogin recorded, including both successful and failed attempts.
An authentication event is what IBM Verify records when someone presents an authentication method. A single sign-in raises more than one: the password is one event, a second factor is another.

title: Authentication Events
text:
Calculation
Sum failed_logins and successful_logins over the selected reporting period.
To track volume over time, bin the same sum by week. Truncating from_date to the week groups each day into its Monday-anchored bin, so the result is one authentication event total per Monday-to-Sunday week.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


Overall:
SELECT
    SUM(failed_logins + successful_logins) AS total_authentication_events
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_auth_total_logins
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28';
By week:
SELECT
    date_trunc('week', CAST(from_date AS DATE)) AS week_start,
    SUM(failed_logins + successful_logins) AS total_authentication_events
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_auth_total_logins
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
-- date_trunc('week', ...) anchors each bin to its Monday
GROUP BY date_trunc('week', CAST(from_date AS DATE))
ORDER BY week_start;


Overall:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_auth_total_logins")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-05-28")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    total_authentication_events = sum(failed_logins + successful_logins, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
By week:
tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_auth_total_logins")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-05-28")
  ) |>
  # floor_date(..., "week") translates to Athena's date_trunc('week', ...),
  # which anchors each bin to its Monday
  mutate(week_start = floor_date(as.Date(from_date), "week")) |>
  group_by(week_start) |>
  summarise(
    total_authentication_events = sum(failed_logins + successful_logins, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(week_start)

title: Authentication Events
text:
Interpretation notes
This counts authentication events. It does not count sign-ins, and it does not count people. A single sign-in that uses a second factor records more than one successful event (see the events_auth_total_logins caveat), so the total runs ahead of how often people actually signed in. No table in the catalog counts sign-ins directly. Use a unique-user metric when the question is about reach. In the weekly view, the first and last weeks of the reporting window are usually partial (the window rarely starts or ends on a Monday), so a low count in a boundary week may reflect fewer days rather than a real dip in volume.

title: Sign-up Email Verification Rate
text:
The proportion of email one-time-code entries that succeeded over a selected reporting period.
During sign-up, CanadaLogin sends a code to the new user’s email address to check that they control it. IBM Verify records this as the email_otp factor, but it is not a second factor: it happens before the account exists, and nobody signs in with it. That is why it is left out of MFA Success Rate and the other sign-in factor metrics, and measured here on its own.
A small share of email_otp events carry a user, so the account already existed and they are not sign-up checks. They are most likely the same check when an existing user changes their email address. The summary table cannot separate them. For the exact split, filter the raw stream on performedby_type = 'api'; see mfa_activity.

title: Sign-up Email Verification Rate
text:
Calculation
Restrict to mfa_type = 'email_otp'. Divide the sum of count where result = 'success' by the sum of count where result is 'success' or 'failure'. Exclude sent rows from both: they are codes issued, not outcomes.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    CAST(SUM(count) FILTER (WHERE result = 'success') AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(SUM(count), 0) AS sign_up_email_verification_rate
FROM ibm_verify_events_transformed.events_mfa_activity
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-05-28'
  AND mfa_type = 'email_otp'
  -- outcomes only; a "sent" row is a code issued
  AND result IN ('success', 'failure');


tbl(con, in_schema("ibm_verify_events_transformed", "events_mfa_activity")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(from_date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(from_date) <= as.Date("2026-05-28"),
    mfa_type == "email_otp",
    # outcomes only; a "sent" row is a code issued
    result %in% c("success", "failure")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    sign_up_email_verification_rate =
      sum(if_else(result == "success", as.double(count), 0), na.rm = TRUE) /
        sum(count, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

title: Sign-up Email Verification Rate
text:
Interpretation notes
The rate is a proportion between 0 and 1, counted per entry: someone who mistypes the code once and then gets it right adds one failure and one success. It does not count people who were sent a code and never entered one; those are sign-ups abandoned at the email step, and show up only as sent rows.

In reporting language, prefer sign-in over login. The underlying IBM Verify field may be called total_logins, but “sign-ins” is preferred (and often enforced) when talking about CanadaLogin.

Scope

title: SLA First-Response Breach Rate
text:
The proportion of PSOM tickets that missed the “Time to first response” SLA, based on the latest snapshot.
This metric is useful for monitoring whether the team is meeting initial response commitments. Only tickets where the SLA clock started are included; tickets with no clock (e.g., non-service-request issue types or tickets created before the SLA scheme was configured) are excluded.

title: SLA First-Response Breach Rate
text:
Calculation
From jira.psom_sla, filter to the most recent date partition, to sla = 'first_response', and to rows where breached is not null (i.e., the clock started). Divide the count of rows where breached is true by the total count of those rows.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


SELECT
    COUNT(*) AS total_sla_tickets,
    SUM(CASE WHEN breached THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS breached_count,
    CAST(SUM(CASE WHEN breached THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS DOUBLE)
        / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0) AS breach_rate
FROM jira.psom_sla
WHERE date = (SELECT MAX(date) FROM jira.psom_sla)
  AND sla = 'first_response'
  AND breached IS NOT NULL;


psom_sla <- tbl(con, in_schema("jira", "psom_sla"))
latest_date <- psom_sla |> summarise(d = max(date, na.rm = TRUE)) |> pull(d)

psom_sla |>
  filter(
    as.Date(date) == as.Date(latest_date),
    sla == "first_response",
    !is.na(breached)
  ) |>
  summarise(
    total_sla_tickets = n(),
    breached_count    = sum(as.integer(breached), na.rm = TRUE),
    breach_rate       = sum(as.integer(breached), na.rm = TRUE) / as.double(n())
  )

title: SLA First-Response Breach Rate
text:
Interpretation notes
The rate is a proportion between 0 and 1. Tickets whose clock never started (null breached) are excluded from both numerator and denominator. Check total_sla_tickets to understand the sample size underlying the rate.
A breach means the ticket missed its own goal, which is set per ticket and counted in working hours (09:00 to 17:00). A ticket that is still waiting for a first response and is inside its goal is recorded as not breached (false), the same as a ticket that met the SLA. The rate on a live snapshot is therefore a lower bound: some of those open tickets may still breach before they are answered. It is most meaningful once the snapshot’s tickets are largely resolved.

The rate is a proportion between 0 and 1. Tickets whose clock never started (null breached) are excluded from both numerator and denominator. Check total_sla_tickets to understand the sample size underlying the rate.
The goal is set per ticket (16, 24, 40 and 72 working hours all occur), so a breach means the ticket missed its own target, not a shared one. A ticket that is still open and inside its goal is recorded as not breached (false), the same as a ticket that met the SLA. The rate on a live snapshot is therefore a lower bound: some of those open tickets may still breach before they are resolved. It is most meaningful once the snapshot’s tickets are largely resolved.
