title: Tickets Opened, Closed, and Open
text: How many PSOM tickets were opened and closed each week, how many were still open at the end of it, and how long a ticket typically stays open.

title: Tickets Opened, Closed, and Open
text:
Calculation
Count every ticket ever seen, not the newest snapshot. A ticket archived out of Jira leaves the board, so the newest jira.psom partition no longer has it. Reading only that partition makes it vanish from the history, as if it was never opened or closed. Take every key from every partition instead.

Opened on the date in created.
Closed on the earliest status_changed of any row where the ticket is Done, Canceled, or Ready to archive, across all partitions. Earliest, because a ticket that went Done and was later moved to Ready to archive keeps the day it was done.
Open at the end of a week if it was opened on or before the week’s last day and not closed by then.

Weeks run Monday to Sunday. Leave off the current week: it is not over, so its counts read short.
Both timestamps carry a UTC offset; their first 10 characters are the local date.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


By week:
WITH tickets AS (
    -- every ticket in any partition, so archived ones stay in the history
    SELECT key, MIN(CAST(substr(created, 1, 10) AS DATE)) AS created_on
    FROM jira.psom
    GROUP BY key
),
closed AS (
    -- the earliest day the ticket was seen in a closed status
    SELECT key, MIN(CAST(substr(status_changed, 1, 10) AS DATE)) AS closed_on
    FROM jira.psom
    WHERE status IN ('Done', 'Canceled', 'Ready to archive')
    GROUP BY key
),
weeks AS (
    -- Mondays of whole weeks; set the reporting window here
    SELECT CAST(d AS DATE) AS week_start, CAST(date_add('day', 6, d) AS DATE) AS week_end
    FROM UNNEST(sequence(DATE '2026-06-29', DATE '2026-09-28', INTERVAL '7' DAY)) AS w(d)
)

SELECT
    w.week_start,
    count_if(t.created_on BETWEEN w.week_start AND w.week_end) AS opened,
    count_if(c.closed_on BETWEEN w.week_start AND w.week_end) AS closed,
    count_if(t.created_on <= w.week_end
             AND (c.closed_on IS NULL OR c.closed_on > w.week_end)) AS open_at_week_end
FROM weeks w
CROSS JOIN tickets t
LEFT JOIN closed c ON t.key = c.key
GROUP BY w.week_start
ORDER BY w.week_start;
Median days open:
WITH tickets AS (
    SELECT key, MIN(CAST(substr(created, 1, 10) AS DATE)) AS created_on
    FROM jira.psom
    GROUP BY key
),
closed AS (
    SELECT key, MIN(CAST(substr(status_changed, 1, 10) AS DATE)) AS closed_on
    FROM jira.psom
    WHERE status IN ('Done', 'Canceled', 'Ready to archive')
    GROUP BY key
),
ages AS (
    -- closed in the 28 days to 2026-09-30, or still open on it; set the window here
    SELECT
        date_diff('day', t.created_on, COALESCE(c.closed_on, DATE '2026-09-30')) AS days_open,
        c.closed_on IS NULL OR c.closed_on > DATE '2026-09-30' AS still_open
    FROM tickets t
    LEFT JOIN closed c ON t.key = c.key
    WHERE t.created_on <= DATE '2026-09-30'
      AND (c.closed_on IS NULL OR c.closed_on > DATE '2026-09-02')
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT
        days_open,
        row_number() OVER (ORDER BY days_open) AS position,
        COUNT(*) OVER () AS tickets
    FROM ages
)

SELECT
    -- the median: the middle age, or the mean of the middle two
    AVG(CAST(days_open AS DOUBLE)) FILTER (
        WHERE position IN (FLOOR((tickets + 1) / 2.0), CEIL((tickets + 1) / 2.0))
    ) AS median_days_open,
    MAX(tickets) AS tickets,
    (SELECT count_if(still_open) FROM ages) AS still_open
FROM ranked;


By week:
psom <- tbl(con, in_schema("jira", "psom")) |>
  select(key, status, created, status_changed) |>
  collect()

# every ticket in any partition, so archived ones stay in the history
tickets <- psom |>
  group_by(key) |>
  summarise(created_on = min(as.Date(substr(created, 1, 10))), .groups = "drop")

# the earliest day the ticket was seen in a closed status
closed <- psom |>
  filter(status %in% c("Done", "Canceled", "Ready to archive")) |>
  group_by(key) |>
  summarise(closed_on = min(as.Date(substr(status_changed, 1, 10))), .groups = "drop")

board <- left_join(tickets, closed, by = "key")

# Mondays of whole weeks; set the reporting window here
tibble(week_start = seq(as.Date("2026-06-29"), as.Date("2026-09-28"), by = "7 days")) |>
  mutate(week_end = week_start + 6) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(
    opened = sum(board$created_on >= week_start & board$created_on <= week_end),
    closed = sum(board$closed_on >= week_start & board$closed_on <= week_end, na.rm = TRUE),
    open_at_week_end = sum(board$created_on <= week_end &
                             (is.na(board$closed_on) | board$closed_on > week_end))
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(week_start, opened, closed, open_at_week_end)
Median days open:
psom <- tbl(con, in_schema("jira", "psom")) |>
  select(key, status, created, status_changed) |>
  collect()

tickets <- psom |>
  group_by(key) |>
  summarise(created_on = min(as.Date(substr(created, 1, 10))), .groups = "drop")

closed <- psom |>
  filter(status %in% c("Done", "Canceled", "Ready to archive")) |>
  group_by(key) |>
  summarise(closed_on = min(as.Date(substr(status_changed, 1, 10))), .groups = "drop")

as_of <- as.Date("2026-09-30")

# closed in the 28 days to as_of, or still open on it; set the window here
left_join(tickets, closed, by = "key") |>
  filter(created_on <= as_of, is.na(closed_on) | closed_on > as_of - 28) |>
  mutate(
    days_open = as.integer(coalesce(closed_on, as_of) - created_on),
    still_open = is.na(closed_on) | closed_on > as_of
  ) |>
  summarise(
    median_days_open = median(days_open),
    tickets = n(),
    still_open = sum(still_open)
  )

title: Tickets Opened, Closed, and Open
text:
Interpretation notes
Why open tickets count in the median. Taking only the tickets closed in the window leaves out the slow ones still sitting in the queue, so the median looks better than the service is. Taking the tickets opened in the window has the same fault: the ones still open have no age yet. Tickets closed in the window plus every ticket still open is the fix: each slow ticket counts at the age it has reached.
Close dates are approximate. Many tickets were never caught at Done; they went straight to Ready to archive when the board was tidied, so their close date is the tidying day. The weekly snapshot until 2026-09-28 also means a status held for less than a week may never have been seen.
Test tickets are on the board and cannot be filtered cleanly; counts include them.

title: Additional Notes
text:
A sign-in count measures events. One person can sign in multiple times.

title: Additional Notes
section: Daily unique users are not the same as period unique users
text:
Daily unique users are not the same as period unique users
Summing daily unique users gives a measure of user-days, not distinct people over the full period.
For distinct people over a longer period, use a cumulative unique user field such as mtd_unique_users or ytd_unique_users.
For a plain-language explanation of why the daily figures cannot be added, and why no unique-user count exists for an arbitrary window, see Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up.

title: Additional Notes
section: Metrics can be reported over different timespans
text:
Metrics can be reported over different timespans
Most metrics are meaningful over more than one window. The three standard reporting windows are month-to-date, year-to-date, and since the April 22, 2026 public launch. How you select a window depends on the kind of metric.
Additive metrics (sign-ins, MFA attempts, success rates, averages) are computed by aggregating daily rows, so the window is just the date bounds in the WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '<start>' AND DATE '<end>' clause. The same query covers any window; only the start date changes:

Month-to-date: first of the current month (for example, 2026-06-01)
Year-to-date: 2026-01-01
Since launch: 2026-04-22

Set the end date to the reporting date.
Cumulative unique-user metrics cannot be derived by filtering a date range, because summing daily unique_users counts user-days, not distinct people. Instead, pick the pre-computed column that matches the window and take its latest value:

Month-to-date: mtd_unique_users
Year-to-date: ytd_unique_users

Never sum these cumulative columns across rows.
There is no since-launch unique-user column. Additive metrics, such as authentication events, SSO events, and MFA attempts, can be summed over any window back to launch.

title: Additional Notes
section: Weighted averages should be used for call centre averages
text:
Weighted averages should be used for call centre averages
When calculating average call length or average delay across multiple weeks, use a weighted average based on calls_answered.
A simple average of weekly averages may give too much influence to low-volume weeks.

title: Additional Notes
section: Internal applications should usually be excluded from external adoption reporting
text:
Internal applications should usually be excluded from external adoption reporting
Which applications count as internal is recorded in rp.service.is_internal, not in this document. Resolve it through rp.alias, which maps the application names IBM Verify and Google Analytics use back to a single service:
SELECT al.alias
FROM   rp.alias al
JOIN   rp.service s ON al.rp_id = s.rp_id
WHERE  s.is_internal
Query the list rather than pasting it into a filter. A service is reclassified by editing the source spreadsheet, and a query holding its own copy of the list will not notice. The same subquery works as a NOT IN in SQL and as an anti_join() in dbplyr; both forms appear in SSO Events by Application.
Whether to exclude internal applications at all depends on the reporting question.

title: Additional Notes
section: External services with no recent traffic can be treated as inactive
text:
External services with no recent traffic can be treated as inactive
An external service with no SSO events in the last three months can be treated as inactive and left out of reporting, such as a count of integrated services or a table with one row per service. It is still a relying party; it has nothing to report. Say so wherever a count of services appears, because a reader cannot tell a dropped service from one that never existed.

title: Additional Notes
section: The user ID “UNKNOWN” counts as one user
text:
The user ID “UNKNOWN” counts as one user
Some IBM Verify events carry the literal user ID "UNKNOWN" in place of a pseudonymized one. The summary tables count it as one user in unique_users, mtd_unique_users, and ytd_unique_users. Recipes that read the raw stream do the same, so the two agree. It moves any count by at most one.

title: Mean Time to Resolution
text: The average time, in minutes, from when an incident is detected to when it is fully resolved.

title: Mean Time to Resolution
text:
Calculation
Average mttr_detected_resolved (minutes from detected_at to resolved_at, precomputed in the table) across the incidents whose detected_at falls in the reporting window, from sre.mttr_current. Because the incident timestamps are stored as America/Toronto strings rather than native dates, the window casts the YYYY-MM-DD prefix of detected_at to a DATE instead of filtering a from_date column. Unresolved incidents have a null mttr_detected_resolved and are excluded from the average.
To break the figure out for service-level reporting, group the same average by severity.






NoteExample queries






SQLR


Overall:
SELECT
    AVG(mttr_detected_resolved) AS mean_time_to_resolution
FROM sre.mttr_current
-- set the reporting window on detected_at; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(substr(detected_at, 1, 10) AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-06-26';
By severity:
SELECT
    severity,
    AVG(mttr_detected_resolved) AS mean_time_to_resolution
FROM sre.mttr_current
-- set the reporting window on detected_at; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE CAST(substr(detected_at, 1, 10) AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-06-26'
GROUP BY severity
ORDER BY severity;


Overall:
tbl(con, in_schema("sre", "mttr_current")) |>
  # set the reporting window on detected_at; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(str_sub(detected_at, 1, 10)) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(str_sub(detected_at, 1, 10)) <= as.Date("2026-06-26")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    mean_time_to_resolution = mean(mttr_detected_resolved, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
By severity:
tbl(con, in_schema("sre", "mttr_current")) |>
  # set the reporting window on detected_at; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    as.Date(str_sub(detected_at, 1, 10)) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(str_sub(detected_at, 1, 10)) <= as.Date("2026-06-26")
  ) |>
  group_by(severity) |>
  summarise(
    mean_time_to_resolution = mean(mttr_detected_resolved, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(severity)

title: Mean Time to Resolution
text:
Interpretation notes
The figure is in minutes; divide by 60 for hours. It is a mean, so a single very long incident can pull it up sharply, especially given how few incidents there are in any window. Read it alongside the incident count, and consider a median or a Sev1-only cut when one outlier dominates.
The window is anchored on detected_at, so an incident counts in the period it began, even if it was resolved in a later period. severity is unvalidated free text in the source sheet, so the grouped view reflects whatever values were typed (expect the occasional typo or spacing drift).

title: Site Response Time
text: The average HTTP response time for each monitored CanadaLogin site, aggregated over rolling windows from five-minute ping data.

title: Site Response Time
text:
Calculation
Filter to the most recent date partition and read the precomputed rolling-window response time columns from sre.uptime_summary. Each response_*_ms column is the mean response time in milliseconds over all five-minute pings in the named window.
For a single-ping point-in-time reading (not an average), use sre.uptime_timeseries.response_ms instead.






Warning



Upstream monitoring gap (July 28 – September 23, 2026): External synthetic health checks in cds-snc/status-statut halted during this ~8-week window. Because zero pings were executed, average latency collapsed to response_day_ms = 0 (a physical impossibility for real HTTP traffic).

When querying historical response time trends or averages, filter out unmonitored days using WHERE response_day_ms > 0.









NoteExample queries






SQLR


Latest snapshot, all sites, all rolling windows:
SELECT
    slug,
    lang,
    status,
    response_day_ms,
    response_week_ms,
    response_month_ms,
    response_year_ms,
    response_alltime_ms
FROM sre.uptime_summary
WHERE date = (SELECT MAX(date) FROM sre.uptime_summary)
ORDER BY slug;
Trend over time, weekly average response time for a specific site:
SELECT
    date,
    response_week_ms,
    response_alltime_ms
FROM sre.uptime_summary
-- set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
WHERE slug = 'canada-login-website-en'
  AND CAST(date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-06-30'
  -- exclude dates where upstream monitoring was inactive
  AND response_day_ms > 0
ORDER BY date;


Latest snapshot, all sites, all rolling windows:
uptime_s <- tbl(con, in_schema("sre", "uptime_summary"))
latest_date <- uptime_s |> summarise(d = max(date, na.rm = TRUE)) |> pull(d)

uptime_s |>
  filter(as.Date(date) == as.Date(latest_date)) |>
  select(slug, lang, status, response_day_ms, response_week_ms,
         response_month_ms, response_year_ms, response_alltime_ms) |>
  arrange(slug)
Trend over time, weekly average response time for a specific site:
tbl(con, in_schema("sre", "uptime_summary")) |>
  # set the reporting window; see the timespans note in cookbook/notes.qmd
  filter(
    slug == "canada-login-website-en",
    as.Date(date) >= as.Date("2026-01-01"),
    as.Date(date) <= as.Date("2026-06-30"),
    # exclude dates where upstream monitoring was inactive
    response_day_ms > 0
  ) |>
  select(date, response_week_ms, response_alltime_ms) |>
  arrange(date)

title: Site Response Time
text:
Interpretation notes
Response times are averages computed from all 288 five-minute pings in the window. Single-measurement spikes are smoothed out. During outage periods, pings that time out contribute high response times or are excluded depending on the upptime implementation, so treat response time trends during known outage windows with caution.
During the July 28 – September 23, 2026 monitoring outage, response_day_ms was recorded as 0, serving as a sentinel value. Failing to filter out these dates (response_day_ms > 0) will artificially drag down historical average latency figures.

title: Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up
text:
A unique-user figure counts people, not sign-ins. That makes it behave differently from most numbers in this cookbook. This page explains the two rules that follow, why they exist, and what to ask for instead.
The short version:

title: Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up
section: One week, two ways of counting
text:
One week, two ways of counting
Here is a week of sign-ins by five people. A dot means that person signed in that day.



A grid of five people against seven days, with a dot on each day a person signed in. The daily count of people is 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1. Adding those gives 12, but there are only 5 names.


Both totals are correct. They answer different questions.

12 is the number of person-days: the number of times someone showed up on a given day. Amira counts five times because she came on five days.
5 is the number of people. Amira counts once no matter how many days she came.

The daily unique-user figure is the “people that day” row. Adding that row up gives person-days, not people. So a report that says “we had 12 unique users this week” would be wrong. The true figure is 5.

title: Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up
section: Why the totals do not add
text:
Why the totals do not add
Adding two unique-user figures only works if nobody appears in both. In practice, the regular users appear in every period, and they get counted again each time.



Two overlapping circles. The Monday circle holds Ben and Amira, the Tuesday circle holds Amira and Chloe. Amira sits in the overlap.


To get the true figure you need to know who was in the overlap. That means knowing which people were behind each count, and we do not have that information.
The same thing happens across applications. Someone who uses two integrated applications is one unique user for CanadaLogin overall but appears in each application’s own count. Adding up the applications’ figures over-counts them, and the overall CanadaLogin figure will always be smaller than that sum.

title: Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up
section: What we keep, and what we do not
text:
What we keep, and what we do not
IBM Verify, the service behind CanadaLogin sign-in, is the only system that knows who signed in. It keeps that per-person record for 90 days, then deletes it.
Our data warehouse never receives the per-person record at all. That is a deliberate choice, required by the security and privacy rules CanadaLogin operates under. Each day, IBM Verify counts up the day’s activity and hands us the finished numbers: how many people signed in that day, and how many distinct people have signed in so far this month. We store the numbers. We do not store, and cannot look up, who was behind them.



A timeline showing IBM Verify holding the per-person record for only the last 90 days, above three rows showing what the warehouse keeps: a figure per day, a figure per calendar month, and a custom window marked as not stored and not rebuildable.


This is why a unique-user count exists only for the windows we asked for in advance. If nobody asked for “April 22 to June 30” before those days happened, the count was never made. We cannot make it now, because we hold no names to count, and after 90 days neither does IBM Verify.

title: Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up
section: What you can and cannot ask for
text:
What you can and cannot ask for







Question
Can we answer it?




How many people signed in yesterday?
Yes. We have a figure for every day.


How many people signed in in July?
Yes. We have a figure for every calendar month.


How many people signed in on average per day in July?
Yes. Averaging the daily figures is fine; it is adding them that misleads.


How many people signed in from April 22 to June 30?
No. That window was not set up in advance, and it cannot be rebuilt.


How many people signed in in the second quarter?
No. A quarter is three monthly figures, and monthly figures cannot be added.


How many people used Application A or Application B?
No. Each application has its own figure, and the two overlap.


How many people have signed in this year?
Not reliably. See the next section.



Person-days, the “12” above, is a legitimate measure on its own. It is the right denominator for a rate such as calls per active user, where each day’s activity should count. Just do not present it as a number of people.

title: Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up
text:
Year-to-date and 365-day figures
The tables also carry a year-to-date figure and a rolling 365-day figure. Both are calculated by IBM Verify over a window longer than the 90 days of per-person data it holds, so they cannot be right. The year-to-date figure has been seen going down from one day to the next, which a true cumulative count cannot do. Do not quote either figure until the pipeline is fixed. The daily and monthly figures are unaffected because both windows fit inside 90 days.
